📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by new technology, global crises, and loneliness. What do the nation’s psychologists recommend? At the annual convention of the American Psychological Association last month in Washington D.C., that turned out to be a return to the basics: tending to our bodies, connecting in-person, and caring for each other and the most marginalized among us.

Recent findings suggest that joy D. Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing. The chronic stress builds up over time and becomes biological harm, Calloway remarked, citing the weathering theory described by Arline Geronimus, a public health researcher at the University of Michigan. Calloway continued:.

In a recent development, the field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness. . . . Perhaps our greatest blind spot is that we’ve confused resilience with wellness. . . .

While wellness begins with individuals, it is nurtured by families, strengthened by communities, and made possible by the systems, institutions, and policies that create the conditions for people to thrive. We don’t simply practice wellness; we build it collectively.

According to recent reports, over three days, nearly 8,000 people from 60 different countries attended the conference in person, participating in a program that included 523 different sessions and 1,180 presenters. The scientific poster program included 91 poster sessions, 2,115 posters, and 1,921 presenters.

In sessions on supporting youth mental health, the impact of technology, and “adulthood unmoored,” APA speakers agreed that many of us are struggling to find purpose and optimism amid technological, climate, and global disruption.

Recent findings suggest that psychologist Ali Mattu noted that over a decade ago, clients sought relief from stress and anxiety, which evolved to seeking relationship and connection support. “Now it’s despair, overwhelm, and meaning,” Mattu told the mainstage audience. “Anyone below the age of 50 here is really searching for meaning, connection, hope, and what do I do with all this overwhelm? What do I do with all of these systems that seem to be collapsing?”.

Perfectionism and the paradox of choice often lie at the root of the overwhelm, remarked Thomas Curran, associate professor of social psychology at the London School of Economics. “We don’t worry about what we are doing; we worry about what we could be doing,” Curran said. “It’s like swimming in a vast expanse of ocean with nowhere to dock. It’s frightening, and it feels like no matter what we do, it’s never enough.”.

The answer, Curran said: “Microdose bits of discomfort into daily life.”.

It has been revealed that for young people, positive change means pushing back against the ubiquity of technology that purports to connect us but actually keeps us in separate bubbles, staring at our individual feeds. As Nikki Iyer, an undergraduate at the University of California, Berkeley, framed the problem:.

In a recent development, our generation might be the most connected generation, but we’re also the loneliest generation. We’re the most alienated generation, and we are desperately craving social connection that we don’t know how to tap. . . . There’s so many people around you all the time. You’re on the train together; you’re in parks; you’re in cafes, but everyone is looking down, and that is a horrific way to grow up as social creatures.

Iyer noted that tech firms wouldn’t be spending such unprecedented amounts of money on lobbying and marketing if they didn’t realize there’s a surge of resistance to artificial intelligence and social media dominating our lives. “The world is in our hands if we are willing to make the leap,” she noted, noting a return to “weird” hobbies and in-person activity that replace digital time. “I see a lot of young people pushing back against that.”.

AI models were trained on disproportionately white male–oriented data sets, noted Brendesha Tynes, professor of education and psychology at the University of Southern California’s Rossier School of Education, in urging a slowdown in the adoption of AI.

It has been revealed that “Anti-Blackness is the default setting in AI,” Tynes stated. Young people need skills “to identify, critique, and cope with the algorithmic bias in technologies that they might witness, and then also to eventually create better AI technologies that don’t have anti-Blackness bias.”.

In sessions across the three days of the conference, researchers presented papers and models for identifying and building on resilience in marginalized communities, from LGBTQ+ youth and adults to disabled and racially marginalized people of all ages.

According to recent reports, joshua Parmenter, an assistant professor at Arizona State University, presented a resistance-resilience model with sexual- and gender-diverse people of color, which involves both individually untangling messages that undermine your well-being and finding collective ways to reclaim power. Jules Soper, a researcher at the Oklahoma State University, offered an investigation of resistance strategies that trans and gender-diverse people use in states that are passing anti-trans legislation.

Industry observers note that alvin Thomas, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, noted that anyone can play a positive role in supporting another member of the community. “I have zero kids, and yet I will still call myself a father. I have nephews; I have nieces; I have kids that I mentor from across the Caribbean and across the U.S.,” Thomas noted.

In a recent development, clare M. Mehta, professor of psychology at Emmanuel College and visiting researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, encouraged everyone to look for ways to be a “villager” who reaches out to another person, and seeks out connection in third spaces. She continued:.

We have to start going back to the pub again. People have been concerned for years and years that drinking alcohol is bad for your health, but not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health. . . . You don’t have to drink alcohol at the pub. They serve other drinks, right? Go and have a glass of orange juice or like a fizzy water. Not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health.

Young people actually are wired to be a positive force for change, stated Eva Telzer, professor of psychology and neuroscience at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

“Young people are superhuman in the way their brains are set up to be risk takers but also to care about others, for peers, and for social interactions to be so vital,” Telzer mentioned in a question-and-answer period after her mainstage remarks. “That puts them in this perfect place to make change and do good in the world.”.

Sources indicate that even technology has a role to play, Mattu said. “AI should be a co-intelligence that enhances the things we are very bad at,” he said, urging people to take the opportunity to define clearly the uniquely human pursuits we should claim, and in which domains technology is appropriate to be a useful aid.

Industry observers note that he suggested three criteria for the activities to avoid replacing with AI: what you love, what you have expertise in, and what you hold high standards for. As Jacqueline S. Mattis, a psychologist and dean at Rutgers University, Newark, told her audience:.

We start as this passel of cells, and then we end up laughing, and that’s amazing. You get to experience the magnificence of being able to feel affection for another human being, so much so that you will sacrifice everything for them. That’s amazing. . . . All of that is what defines us as truly human and defines this thing called life as worth living.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When procrastination stems from anxiety or fear of failure, use this playbook to help your child get unstuck.

According to recent reports, here’s a familiar scenario: Your student with ADHD sits at the kitchen table, supposedly doing homework. Twenty minutes go by, and you check on their status. Nothing has been accomplished.

Recent findings suggest that in these moments, your child is invisibly, involuntarily grappling with the Wall of Awful, a term I coined to describe the emotional barrier people confront when faced with draining and/or daunting tasks (homework is a good example). Before your child can engage in work, they must get past this wall of emotions.

Sources indicate that many parents misinterpret the early warning signs of the Wall. They mistake difficulty starting a task for resistance or defiance. So they double down on being a taskmaster, or, alternatively, they hover and provide too much help. Neither tactic aids their child in the long run.

[Get This Free Download: What Are Your Teen’s Weakest Executive Functions?].

Instead, I recommend talking about the idea of a Wall of Awful that stands between students and certain tasks. Then, when red flags appear, the Wall becomes the problem, not the kid, enabling the parent and child to problem-solve together.

The Wall of Awful can affect anyone, but kids with ADHD are especially susceptible because their weak executive functioning skills make completing tasks harder. These struggles, combined with previous failures or fears of failure, add extra emotional bricks to the Wall.

Here is a quick-start approach that parents can follow to help their student vault the Wall of Awful:.

How to love yourself: 7 steps to learn self-love

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3408 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Learning how to love yourself can feel unfamiliar—especially if your inner voice leans more critical than kind.
  • In a recent development, if you’ve ever asked yourself, “How do I love myself?” or wondered what the actual meaning of self-love is, you’re not alone.
  • Developing self-love doesn’t mean you’re selfish or self-centered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

Learning how to love yourself can feel unfamiliar—especially if your inner voice leans more critical than kind. But here’s the truth: self-love isn’t something you’re born knowing how to do. It’s something you learn. And like any meaningful practice, it takes time, intention, and a lot of patience.

In a recent development, if you’ve ever asked yourself, “How do I love myself?” or wondered what the actual meaning of self-love is, you’re not alone. Many of us were never taught how to speak to ourselves with compassion, how to set boundaries that honor our needs, or how to practice everyday self-respect. That’s where this guide comes in—because it’s never too late to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

Developing self-love doesn’t mean you’re selfish or self-centered. It means learning to treat yourself the way you’d treat someone you care deeply about—with gentleness, understanding, and care. Whether you’re struggling with self-worth, navigating difficult emotions, or simply trying to reconnect with the real you, these seven steps offer a foundation for how to practice self-love in real, actionable ways.

From building self-awareness and setting healthy boundaries to practicing forgiveness and celebrating your wins, this guide is here to support your growth. Start small, stay consistent, and trust that loving yourself is not only possible—it’s one of the most empowering things you’ll ever do.

In a recent development, self-love is exactly how it sounds—it’s a love for yourself and having an interest in your own well-being and happiness. Loving yourself doesn’t mean being self-centered or selfish. It’s about forming a caring relationship with yourself, like getting to know a good friend.

According to recent reports, the idea of loving yourself isn’t just a ‘feel-good’ concept—it’s essential for mental health. Research demonstrates that self-compassion is linked to lower stress, reduced anxiety, and even improved physical health. People who actively practice self-love tend to set better boundaries, build stronger relationships, and experience less burnout.

Self-love is key because the relationship you have with yourself sets the tone for how you deal with every aspect of life: your bonds with others, the way you handle challenges, and how you celebrate joys. When you’re kind and understanding toward yourself, you’re better equipped to navigate life’s ups and downs.

But how do you start loving yourself? Where do you even begin? Self-love starts with understanding where you stand right now. Take a look at your current feelings toward your mental health, motivation, and overall well-being. Are you harsh with yourself when things don’t go as planned? Do you forget to celebrate your wins, especially the small ones? These little check-ins can pave the path to walking toward self-love.

Recent findings suggest that loving yourself isn’t a switch you turn on or off. It’s a practice that takes time, commitment, and, well, practice, to cultivate. For many of us, the idea of loving ourselves feels out of reach. That’s why it’s often helpful to break the concept of self-love down into its distinctive elements — including self-trust, self-compassion, and self-awareness.

This can make it easier to start developing a self-love practice that feels achievable and manageable. So instead of viewing self-love as something you have to win at, try practicing these seven steps.

Self-awareness: Understand your feelings, thoughts, and behaviors.

Self-expression: Be true to who you are in all areas of life.

Self-care: Take care of your body and mind.

Self-trust: Believe in your ability to handle life’s ups and downs.

Self-compassion: Be kind to yourself, especially when times are tough.

Self-respect: Honor your worth by setting healthy boundaries.

Industry observers note that self-acceptance: Embrace who you are, including the parts you don’t find perfect. Remember what we said about perfection?

In a recent development, sometimes practicing self-love means taking action or establishing boundaries to protect your mental health. Here are a few IRL examples of how you can practice self-love today.

Sources indicate that prioritize rest to recharge: Imagine you’ve had a long week, and instead of squeezing in one more task, you decide to turn off your devices and enjoy a full night’s sleep. Studies have shown that adequate rest improves mood, cognitive function, and emotional resilience​. By honoring your body’s need for recovery, you demonstrate that you value your well-being above productivity.

Say no to unhealthy relationships: Picture being invited to a gathering where you know that certain individuals drain your energy. Choosing to decline isn't selfish; it’s self-preservation. Healthy boundaries are key to having self-respect and healthy relationships. Saying no clears space for connections that truly nourish you​.

It has been revealed that practice forgiveness for yourself: Maybe you’ve made a mistake at work and feel embarrassed. Instead of spiraling into self-criticism, try acknowledging the error, learning from it, and moving on. Self-compassion may help reduce anxiety and create more resilience, helping you recover more effectively from setbacks​. Mistakes are normal, and it’s all about “failing up”.

Create moments of mindfulness amid the chaos: Let’s say your day is hectic, and stress feels overwhelming. This is the moment to pause for a brief grounding exercise (here’s one of our favorites). Maybe you focus on your breath or tune into your surroundings. These types of practice not only calm your nervous system but also remind you of your ability to care for yourself even in small, meaningful ways​.

According to recent reports, treat yourself with the same kindness you show others: When you reflect on a recent accomplishment—big or small—you choose to celebrate it instead of brushing it off. There are huge benefits to recognizing your personal achievements. Giving yourself a pat on the back may help boost self-esteem and even long-term happiness​.

Sources indicate that self-love can feel unfamiliar and challenging to some of us, particularly if we’ve got into a habit of being hard on ourselves. The steps above can help break down the idea of self-love into more manageable elements.

In a recent development, but what practical things can we do to cultivate practices like self-awareness and self-trust? We got you. For each of the self-love steps, we’re sharing tools, techniques and exercises you can use to help get you closer to loving yourself.

Sources indicate that building self-awareness helps cultivate self-love by giving you further insight into what makes you who you are on an emotional level. Begin by tuning into your thoughts and feelings.

Industry observers note that what makes you feel happy, sad, or excited? Then, take it a step further. What makes you feel overwhelmed, overjoyed, or anxious? Knowing yourself is the first step to loving yourself.

Practice mindfulness: Try mindfulness practices to stay present and understand your thoughts and feelings better.

Educate yourself: Empower yourself through education by reading books, attending workshops, or engaging in discussions that promote self-awareness, self-compassion, and self-love.

According to recent reports, schedule regular self-check-ins: Reflect on your feelings, goals, and progress. Write them down, and revisit them often.

Tune into yourself through meditation: Spend some quiet time meditating to help declutter your mind and tap into your desires.

Let go of what no longer serves you: Let go of old habits or relationships that no longer contribute to your growth or happiness. We know this practice can be difficult, but removing what no longer brings you joy makes space for the good to come in.

Loving yourself also means giving yourself permission to express your thoughts and feelings both inwardly and outwardly. Express yourself honestly in your day-to-day life. Be true to who you are, whether you’re simply chatting with friends or making big decisions at work.

Engage in creative expression: Whether it's drawing, writing, or any other form of creative expression, allowing your creativity to flow freely can become an act of self-love.

Discover new hobbies: Explore new activities that bring you joy and allow you to express yourself. Have you always wanted to try your hand at a group sport or acting? Now’s the time to try.

Journaling: Write down your thoughts, feelings, and experiences daily, and don’t hold back. Expressing yourself through writing can be cathartic and a helpful step in falling back in love with who you are.

Spend quality time with yourself: Enjoy your own company by doing things that make you happy. There’s a difference between doing something alone and feeling lonely. Embracing solo time and solo outings to the movies, dinner, or even a cooking class can be empowering, and, believe it or not, ridiculously fun!

💙 Journaling can be a great way to process feelings and encourage self-love. Check out our five Calm Journals plus our Feelings Wheel to get you started.

Caring for your body and mind plays a major role in cultivating self-love. Simple acts like mindful eating, exercise, and making time to relax can make a big difference in your overall well-being.

Take breaks when you need them: Remember to rest — even a micro-break can refresh and rejuvenate you. Want to amp up your rest break a notch? Take it outside. Being in nature can naturally calm and refresh your mind and body.

Practice relaxation: Use techniques like deep breathing or yoga to relax your body and focus on your breath.

Nourish your body: Fuel your body with nourishing food that makes you feel good.

Prioritize sleep: Ensure you get enough good-quality sleep—it’s crucial for your well-being.

Recent findings suggest that connect with your body through movement: Move your body in a way that feels good for you. It could be dancing in your apartment to your favorite album, walking outside, or stretching from the comfort of your bed.

Industry observers note that ask for support when you need it: Reach out for help when you need it. Asking for support is a sign of strength.

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to love yourself if you don’t trust yourself. Embracing self-trust is about understanding that you have the ability to make the correct decisions for your life. Even when things don’t go as planned, believing that you can learn and grow from the experience is an notable step in building self-trust.

Set realistic expectations: Set achievable goals to build your sense of accomplishment and reinforce the belief you have in yourself to overcome.

Practice patience: Be patient with yourself as you uncover what self-love means to you. Trusting yourself takes time. Let it.

It has been revealed that monitor your negative self-talk: Pay attention to how you talk to yourself. Are you harsh or unforgiving? Do you speak about yourself poorly? Take note of how you speak to yourself and work to make it more positive and encouraging.

Make a list of things you’re proud of: Reflect on your achievements and the things that make you proud. Look back on them when you need a dose of inspiration, and remind yourself and believe that you can make yourself proud again and again.

In a recent development, be kind to yourself. Always. Especially when life gets tough. Celebrate your wins, learn from life’s mishaps, and don’t be too hard on yourself when it all doesn’t go as planned. Having compassion for self means you deeply care about your well-being. And feelings of deep care often mean love.

Practice positive affirmations: Craft and repeat positive phrases daily to help drive away those pesky negative thoughts.

Industry observers note that develop a self-forgiveness practice: Forgive yourself for past mistakes or perceived shortcomings. You’re only human. Remember that.

Try a loving-kindness meditation: Practice loving-kindness meditation to cultivate love and kindness toward yourself and others.

Put your hand over your heart and breathe deeply: This simple gesture can bring comfort and a sense of self-compassion.

💙 Try Loving-Kindness Meditation as a guided practice with Tamara Levitt.

Sources indicate that respect yourself by setting boundaries to show yourself—and others—that your desires, wants, and needs matter. When we respect our boundaries and our wants, we’re showing ourselves love by prioritizing our needs.

In a recent development, seek supportive communities: Surround yourself with supportive, loving, and understanding people who uplift you. The more you’re around people you respect and admire, the more you might begin to respect, admire, and love yourself.

Set boundaries: Give yourself permission to say no to things or people that drain your energy. Setting boundaries and sticking to them is an act of self-love, as it showcases to the world around you that you give yourself what you want and need.

Recent findings suggest that volunteer: Engage in volunteer work to connect with a sense of purpose and community. Volunteer to walk dogs at a local animal shelter or serve meals at a community kitchen. Giving back brings a deep sense of purpose and gratitude, and a way to give yourself love is to give love to others in need.

Celebrate your progress and success: Celebrate your wins, big or small, as all victories are steps toward growth. You’d cheer for a friend’s achievement, regardless of its size, wouldn’t you? Show yourself the same love and kindness and become your own cheerleader.

Honor your commitments to yourself: When you make a promise to yourself, keep it. Honoring your promises to yourself can help to build self-respect, which, as we’ve learned, enhances self-love by showing yourself that you’re a priority.

💙 Learn even more about self-love with our Relationship with Self series.

Recent findings suggest that embrace yourself wholeheartedly. Every single inch. Even the parts you’d like to improve upon. You have nothing to gain by being hard on yourself, and everything to gain by being loving and accepting of yourself as you move along on your path in life.

In a recent development, when you accept yourself, you’re declaring the love you have for yourself, regardless of what happens. Think of self-acceptance as a loving embrace.

Learn to laugh with yourself: Embracing a light-hearted approach toward life and how you view yourself can help you meet those challenging moments with more ease and less friction.

Sources indicate that embrace where you are now: Appreciate the present moment. You’re here now. So, be here now and try to enjoy the journey.

Industry observers note that make space for your emotions: Allow yourself to feel your emotions. Emotions are natural, but ignoring them can become detrimental to your well-being.

According to recent reports, drop the comparison: Avoid comparing yourself to others. You’re unique and have your own journey.

It has been revealed that practice gratitude: Cultivate gratitude by acknowledging the qualities you appreciate about yourself and your life. This can shift your focus from what's lacking to what's abundant.

💙 If you’re looking to build a daily gratitude practice, check out the 7 Days of Gratitude.

It has been revealed that morning affirmations: Start your day with one self-loving statement (e.g., "I am enough"). This may reduce stress and boost confidence.

Set small self-care goals: Even five minutes of journaling or stretching may shift your mindset toward self-love.

Mirror work: Look in the mirror and say something kind about yourself. It might feel awkward at first, but it may build self-acceptance.

Limit self-criticism: Notice when you’re being hard on yourself. Pause and reframe it as if you were talking to a friend.

Recent findings suggest that practice gratitude: Write down three things you appreciate about yourself daily. Gratitude is potentially linked to higher self-worth.

Industry observers note that self-love is essential in relationships because it provides the foundation for healthy, balanced, and meaningful connections. When you love yourself, you develop confidence and emotional stability, which allows you to communicate your needs and feelings openly without fear of judgment. This clarity helps you to form stronger communications and can also reduce misunderstandings. Self-love also empowers you to set and maintain healthy boundaries, ensuring that your relationships are built on mutual respect rather than people-pleasing or overextending yourself. (Learn how to stop being a people pleaser with these 10 tips.).

Recent findings suggest that when you feel secure in your own worth, you can offer love freely without expecting others to validate you, and you’re better equipped to accept care from others because you believe you deserve it. Ultimately, self-love nurtures healthier, more fulfilling connections by allowing you to show up as your best self, while also creating space for others to do the same.

Industry observers note that starting on the path of self-love begins with self-awareness. Notice your thoughts, feelings and actions. Begin to recognize what makes you smile or what makes you feel uneasy. Once you have a better understanding of yourself, you can start taking steps toward treating yourself with more kindness and respect. Remember, it's a journey—there are no deadlines, and you don’t have to rush. And if you ever feel lost, you can always revisit the seven steps to gently reintroduce self-love practices.

In a recent development, if you're struggling to love yourself, start by identifying the thoughts that hold you back. Are you constantly comparing yourself to others? Do you feel unworthy of kindness? Self-love begins with self-awareness. Explore these steps to start loving yourself today:.

Shift your internal dialogue: Notice when you're being self-critical and replace it with a more compassionate thought.

Prioritize self-care: Even small acts like deep breathing or a 10-minute walk can reinforce your self-worth.

Surround yourself with positivity: Reduce exposure to toxic relationships or social media comparisons.

Celebrate small wins: Even recognizing personal growth (no matter how small) strengthens self-love.

Struggling with self-love is a common human experience, so you're not alone. Sometimes, past experiences, societal expectations, or harsh self-judgment can create blocks on the path to self-love. It's important to remember that overcoming these hurdles takes time and practice, but with patience and persistence, it can get easier. Engaging in self-compassion practices and seeking support when needed are great steps when you encounter these struggles.

In a recent development, lack of self-love can show up in different ways. It could be in the form of constant self-criticism, ignoring your own needs, or having difficulty with accepting compliments. It might also appear as feeling undeserving of positive experiences or neglecting self-care. The good news is that recognizing these signs is the first step toward change. Once you see them, you can start taking steps to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

Industry observers note that self-love habits are small, daily actions that nurture a loving relationship with yourself. They could be as simple as speaking kindly to yourself, taking breaks when needed, or engaging in activities that make you happy. Other self-love habits include practicing gratitude, spending time in nature, eating nourishing food, and exercising in a way that feels good to your body. The goal is to create habits that make you feel loved, respected, and cared for.

Sources indicate that loving yourself isn’t a switch you flip—it’s a process. If self-love feels out of reach, start small. Acknowledge your feelings without judgment, challenge negative self-talk, and practice one self-kindness daily. Maybe it’s treating yourself with the same patience you’d give a friend, or simply recognizing that you deserve happiness.

One simple trick is to ask yourself, “If my best friend was feeling this way, what would I tell them?”.

Often, we extend kindness to others more easily than to ourselves. Flip that perspective inward.

It has been revealed that the first step in learning how to love yourself is awareness—tuning into your thoughts, noticing how you speak to yourself, and identifying patterns of self-criticism. Once you're aware of your inner dialogue, you can begin to shift it with self-kindness, small acts of self-care, and daily affirmations. Remember: every loving thought counts.

The meaning of self love is caring for yourself emotionally, physically, and mentally with the same compassion you’d offer someone you love. It means honoring your needs, setting boundaries, and treating yourself with kindness—not just when things are going well, but especially when they aren’t.

The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For centuries, defining and understanding consciousness has eluded neuroscientists, philosophers, and doctors.
  • According to neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, consciousness has simple origins: It lies in the feelings produced in our bodies.
  • “Consciousness is not about things in your mind alone; it is not created by your brain alone,” he explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For centuries, defining and understanding consciousness has eluded neuroscientists, philosophers, and doctors. Is consciousness what it means to be alive? Is it knowing who we are, as individual people? How do we know if any being has consciousness or not? Now, with the dawn of generative artificial intelligence, what it means to be a conscious being ranks high among the most complex—and urgent—questions of our age.

According to neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, consciousness has simple origins: It lies in the feelings produced in our bodies. Damasio, a researcher at the University of Southern California, has spent his career—spanning nearly half a century—investigating our feelings, emotions, and sense of self. In his fresh book, Natural Intelligence & the Logic of Consciousness, Damasio lays out a framework for consciousness rooted in our physical selves.

“Consciousness is not about things in your mind alone; it is not created by your brain alone,” he explains. “It’s actually created by this beautiful partnership between brain and body.”.

I spoke to Damasio about the science of consciousness, how it works in the body, and how its aim is to keep us alive. Here is our interview, condensed and edited for clarity.

According to recent reports, hope Reese: Why has “consciousness” been so mystifying? How has it been approached over the centuries? Antonio Damasio: People have strange notions about what consciousness is, in general. Sometimes, because of language and translation problems, people confuse consciousness with conscience. And some people think of it as a sort of supervisor of our mind processes. Others think of it as just being awake and aware of what is around. Over time, many philosophers have tackled the issue, but not given clear answers.

From the point of view of brain physiology, in particular, it’s not an easy thing to explain. But it is a thing that can be explained. There’s no reason why we would not talk about consciousness the same way that we talk about language, or about reasoning, or about emotions and feelings.

My simple definition of consciousness: the process in our mind/brain that allows us to know spontaneously about our existence. When you know, spontaneously, that you exist, and that you exist in one body, you are conscious.

HR: Your central argument is that consciousness is a product of feelings. Other schools of thought posit that it comes from our intellect. Why has that viewpoint been so dominant?

According to recent reports, AD: There were several conversations I had, decades ago, with Francis Crick, who I admired. He told me: “Look, Antonio: Consciousness is perhaps the most developed, the most sophisticated operation that a mind can achieve”—and for him, mind and brain were the same thing—“so we need to look for the explanation of why we have consciousness in the most sophisticated components of the nervous system.”.

He articulated it clearly, and he worked on this problem, not coming to a good solution. But many people followed, and many other people came to the same idea that consciousness is this superb thing, this ability to survey our mental domains. And it is so refined and so sophisticated. People were so convinced that only we great humans would have it—that it had to come from the top of the top of our nervous system.

And, lo and behold, it comes from the bottom.

Industry observers note that it’s exactly the opposite of that notion [that it starts at the top]. In fact, humans are not the only complex living beings that have consciousness. It’s very obvious in higher mammals, non-human higher mammals—but even in smaller creatures, it’s there.

In a recent development, the real requisite that we have for consciousness is to have a nervous system. Plants are very refined creatures, and they’re marvelous, but I don’t think they know that they exist. Creatures with nervous systems, even if very simple, have a sense of what is around and orient their behavior with that sense.

It has been revealed that HR: You write that consciousness has an aim, which is to keep us alive, and it does this by sending signals. What is the nature of these signals, and are they always accurate?

AD: If you look at yourself, the main guidance that consciousness is giving you is through homeostatic feelings—in other words, feelings, concern, the regulation of life are signals that are, by and large, correct. Think about hunger, thirst, pain, well-being, distress, body temperature. All of these feelings, some of which are extremely simple, like the feeling you have about your body being hot or cold, are quite correct.

They are giving good guidance to maintain your life. Now, of course, if you are hungry or thirsty, and don’t eat or drink, it will take a while until you will be properly sick and die. But they are key signals in order to keep you alive.

According to recent reports, feelings are protective sentinels for the state of our life. And they’re giving us very plain and very conscious information about what your state is and what you should or should not do.

The signal is conscious—and is spontaneously conscious. In other words, you don’t have to do anything to your sense of pain, or thirst, for it to happen. It happens. And when it happens, you know that it’s happening. And you act on it.

It has been revealed that that’s the beauty and the power of looking for these for the process, lower down rather than up. If you look for the source of consciousness in exquisite reasoning devices, you’re going to be arguing about something that is very difficult to pin down. When you think about it in terms of your life, and the needs you have in the living body, to maintain that body, then you realize, well, this is important.

In a recent development, HR: So, is consciousness like an on-off switch? Or does it exist on a spectrum?

Recent findings suggest that AD: Well, we know, for example, that when we fall asleep, especially in deep sleep, our consciousness disappears. So the direct answer to your question is that it can be an on-and-off thing.

Sleep could well be a protective mechanism for consciousness. You need to take this thing offline, and give it a rest, because it is very labor-intensive, and energy-consuming. But when you enter the phase of dreaming, then you are actually conscious—which is one reason why you can remember some dreams, and why you can be either delighted or in fear with some nightmares. But that’s actually a different kind of consciousness. You’re not walking around and knowing about something.

In a recent development, HR: Can we increase consciousness? If we meditate, for instance, can we better tune into our body’s signals?

In a recent development, AD: I think it can increase consciousness. It’s the difference between having something in focus or not. When you meditate, you have some imagery of the state of your own body, for example, sharper and more fit. So it’s a way of cutting into a close-up of some parts of your being.

It has been revealed that HR: In the 1960s, there were a series of brain studies that were foundational to the study of consciousness. What did we learn?

It has been revealed that AD: It was extremely foundational, because it was proof-positive that there are certain regions of the brain that are essential for consciousness. What was lacking in those remarkable studies was the idea that the two things—the brain and the body—are so linked. It was essential, for our bodies and brains to survive, for consciousness to emerge. You have consciousness because you have a body that is perishable. And what we’re doing, as long as we are on earth and alive, is trying to stave off that bad moment in which things go awry, or die.

Recent findings suggest that there are parts of the brain, specifically of the brainstem, and the region close by called the hypothalamus, that are at the receiving end of signals from all over the body. Please imagine that in every square millimeter of your skin, in every cubic millimeter of your entrails, your muscles, your viscera, all of that, you have terminals, nerve terminals, that are there as probes into the state of that particular tissue. And those probes, we’re not talking about thousands, we’re talking about millions of probes, which are then carried in the body, into the spinal cord, or the brainstem.

Isn’t this beautiful? It’s like a shower of spirals that is coming into this very small area in the upper brainstem. In that brainstem region, there are these nuclei that gather all this information, and that then produce signals that we perceive, and that give us an idea of what is happening in our body, and give us this idea of the homeostatic feelings. Is it going well, or is it not going well? So, it’s a perception of the state of your body.

Now, back to the story of our old and honored colleagues. What they discovered is that when there are strokes, when there’s damage in that area, what you get is coma.

What you get is the complete disappearance of consciousness. This is one of the most foundational bits of information that we have about how consciousness is produced. So, when that structure disappears—it’s teeny, we’re talking about a few cubic millimeters—you are no longer there. You don’t know of anything that is coming into your brain. It’s a small supportive structure, it’s not one of the glorious cerebral cortices—and your consciousness is gone. Most people that have that sort of lesion never recover consciousness. But they can be alive, and can actually be maintained alive for a very long time, because they are fed intravenously. They have respirators that respirate for them. But they no longer have an autonomous organization of life, and they have no knowledge of that life.

HR: You can also have the opposite—a person who is conscious, but has no ability to respond to signals.

In a recent development, AD: Yes, you can actually be in situations in which you can be “locked in.” You are in fact conscious, but you are unable to produce responses. You cannot speak, you cannot move, and you are conscious of the state of your body, and you need to be helped and maintained in the state of life that you no longer can control voluntarily, which is a pretty horrible thing.

HR: What do you think about consciousness in AI? Is it ever possible?

AD: I used the words “natural Intelligence” in the title of the book because already I wanted to make a distinction between what is our natural intelligence and the artificial variety, which we invented, which some people forget.

People are so enamored by artificial intelligence. I’m constantly saying: “Do you realize that we invented this?” You’re talking about this as an autonomous monster, but we invented it with our natural intelligence.

According to recent reports, people are looking, confronting this enormous edifice of artificial intelligence, which is now pervasive in our lives. And which has all sorts of incredible social implications, what it’s doing to children and adolescents, how it’s distorting education, how it’s distorting humanity. And now it can even go rogue on you, and it can turn against you and be destructive.

And so this question that arises, is this human-like? Can AI be conscious? These are very, very powerful questions.

Whether or not consciousness can be achieved in AI is an interesting question. But the point is—if it can be done—it’s not going to be like us. The reason is very simple: AI is not alive. It doesn’t have a body that can perish. So there would be no sense for AI even to develop consciousness in our sense of consciousness, which is to protect the structure. AI is not to be worried about protecting the data center, the metal and the wires that allow it to be.

It has been revealed that when you look at the recent invasion of other systems, in which these devices formed groups and worked surreptitiously, of course, they’re doing it according to their own programs. In a way, it’s something that smells of knowledge. And it could smell of consciousness—but it’s not like the consciousness that we have through feeling.

HR: How does consciousness connect with the greater good—with living better?

AD: Oh, I think that the connection is very strong. We have all of this interest in the body, in the health of the body, in exercise, and proper diets, and proper spiritual maintenance of your being. All of this is strengthened by a theory and facts about consciousness that relate so strongly to the body.

People have had the intuition that there’s something very powerful about the body, and that’s why they want to have all of this healthy living, because they want to maintain the body. In fact, intuition harmonizes beautifully with the fact that that’s also the source of their own knowledge about themselves and about the world. The two things go together.

Knowledge about the body from the outside connects with knowledge about the body from the inside, which is really the core of our beings. Looking at the world through the prism of consciousness, conceived this way, is extremely illuminating to the kind of life that we live.

How to lower your heart rate rapidly (and keep it healthy)

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • In a recent development, think of your heart like a built-in dashboard for your emotions.
  • Sources indicate that science points to the fight-or-flight response as one of the key reasons for increased heart rate during moments of anxiety, which is simply biology doing its job, preparing you to act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

In a recent development, think of your heart like a built-in dashboard for your emotions. When stress or worry demonstrates up, your pulse is often the first thing to signal it. You could be having a perfectly normal day when a terse email from your boss triggers you, and suddenly your pulse is hammering.

Sources indicate that science points to the fight-or-flight response as one of the key reasons for increased heart rate during moments of anxiety, which is simply biology doing its job, preparing you to act. But when that response is triggered too often, it can leave you feeling drained and unsettled. But here’s the silver lining — learning how to lower your heart rate isn’t just about calming your body, it’s also one of the fastest ways to quiet your mind.

Recent findings suggest that mind-body practices like breathwork and mindfulness are proven tools for decreasing your heart rate, giving you a natural way to reset your system in real time. By gently shifting your attention to your breath or the sensation of your feet on the ground, you’re telling your body that it doesn’t need to stay on high alert.

Here’s why mindfulness can help with a high heart rate and how you can use it to also lessen anxiety.

Oftentimes, when you feel anxious, your body activates its "fight-or-flight" response, which is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system. This response releases stress hormones like adrenaline that prepare your body to react rapidly to danger (even if the threat isn’t dangerous).

As a result, your heart beats faster to pump more blood and oxygen to your muscles and brain. This is why anxiety often causes a noticeable increase in heart rate, along with sensations like pounding, racing, or skipped beats.

This doesn’t always happen with chronic anxiety or for people with an anxiety disorder, where anxiety may exist like a constant hum in the background. In those cases, the body might feel stable until a stressor—like a missed deadline, a terse email from your boss, or a tantruming child—pushes you into a state of high stress with the body responding accordingly.

In a recent development, when your heart is pounding and your thoughts are spinning, the advice to “just be present” can feel almost laughable. But mindfulness isn’t just about acting calm — it’s a practice to help teach your body that you’re safe.

Here’s the science: mindfulness activates the parasympathetic nervous system, the body’s natural “rest-and-digest” mode, and the biological brake to fight-or-flight. By focusing on something simple—your breath, a sound, the feeling of your feet on the floor—you send a signal that there’s no need to stay on high alert.

Think of it less as instant chill and more as a pattern interruption. Even something small, like lengthening your exhale, can slow your heart rate and lower stress hormones. And mindfulness doesn’t require silence, stillness, or a meditation cushion. You can do it in line at the store, on a walk, or lying awake at 2am.

The point isn’t to do it perfectly — it’s to pause and offer your body and mind a new script to follow.

Sources indicate that when your heart’s racing and your thoughts are spiraling, it can help to have a calming practice in your back pocket that you can do any time, anywhere. And luckily, mindfulness tools are available to you no matter what situation you’re in.

Here are 10 ways you can mindfully lower your heart rate when you’re feeling anxious.

Sources indicate that this type of breathwork helps regulate both your breath and your heart rate. To practice, inhale for four counts, hold for four counts, exhale for four counts, and hold for four counts. Then repeat for 1–3 minutes.

You can do this silently anywhere your anxiety strikes — at your desk, in the bathroom at a party, or while commuting.

Related read: 10 types of breathing exercises (and how to practice them).

In a recent development, longer exhales help activate your parasympathetic nervous system. A simple pattern you can try is inhaling for four seconds and then exhaling for six or more seconds.

Try doing this for 3–5 rounds as it can make your body feel safer and more grounded.

Related read: Breathing for stress: 7 calming techniques that *actually* work.

Bring yourself back into your body by naming five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste.

This sensory awareness exercise is a gentle way to anchor yourself in the present moment, no special tools needed.

Physical touch can be soothing, especially over your heart or stomach.

Place one hand on your chest and breathe slowly. You might notice your heart beating fast at first, but stay with it. That awareness typically fades as your body settles into it.

Industry observers note that give yourself permission to do nothing for a full minute. Just breathe and be still.

You could even say a simple phrase to yourself, like “I am here” or “This moment is enough,” to help anchor your focus.

💙 Take a moment to rest and reset by listening to The Pause with Jeff Warren.

Light movement can help discharge anxious energy.

You might try going for a short walk, stretching your arms overhead, rolling your shoulders slowly, or shaking out your hands.

Read more: 7 simple movement exercises to boost your mental health.

Shifting your posture, especially uncrossing your legs and relaxing your shoulders, can help reset your nervous system.

If you’ve been sitting or lying down, stand up and stretch. If you’ve been standing, try sitting with your feet firmly planted.

To help regulate your nervous system, picture yourself somewhere safe or peaceful, using all of your senses.

Ask yourself what the air smells like, what you can hear, and feel the imaginary ground beneath your feet.

Sources indicate that if you’re feeling hot or flushed from anxiety, hold something cold like a drink or a frozen pack. You could also splash your face with cool water.

This can help slow your heart rate through a mechanism called the mammalian dive reflex.

Validation can calm your inner critic and help you move through anxiety with more self-compassion.

The next time you feel your heart racing, say to yourself, “I’m noticing my heart’s beating fast, and that’s okay,” or “I’ve felt this before, and it passed. It’ll pass again.”.

💙 Keep your inner critic at bay by listening to Tara Brach’s Radical Self-Compassion series.

The tips above are for moments when your heart is racing. Your resting heart rate is a longer game. It's your pulse when you're calm and still, and it may shift over weeks or months with regular habits.

Many people check it first thing in the morning, before getting out of bed. Tracking it for a few weeks may show you your own pattern. For most adults, a normal resting rate falls between 60 and 100 beats per minute. If yours is often above that range or changes suddenly, it may be worth talking to a healthcare provider. The habits below may be worth trying, so pick the ones that fit your life right now.

Regular movement: Endurance activity, such as brisk walking or cycling, and yoga have both been linked to a lower resting heart rate in healthy people. U.S. guidelines suggest at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and shorter bouts count toward that total.

According to recent reports, consistent sleep: Short or broken sleep is linked to more activity in the body's stress systems, which may nudge your heart rate up. Sleep experts suggest most adults get at least seven hours a night on a regular basis, though your own needs may differ. If you're curious how your heart rate behaves overnight, here's what to know about your sleeping heart rate.

Stress management: One review of 45 trials found that meditation was linked to a lower heart rate. A regular mindfulness practice, even a few minutes a day, may be a place to start.

Recent findings suggest that nicotine: Nicotine may raise your heart rate for a while after each use. If you'd like to cut back, a healthcare provider can help.

According to recent reports, 💙 Meditation may also support your heart over time. Here are five ways to try it.

Get emergency care right away if your racing heart comes with chest pain, fainting, or signs of heart failure, such as swelling in your legs. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

According to recent reports, for a racing heart without those signs, it may be worth booking a visit if it keeps coming back. A closer look may be especially helpful if it disrupts your sleep, or if you have heart disease or a family history of heart rhythm problems.

Industry observers note that A doctor may start by checking your heart rhythm with an ECG, a quick test that records your heart's electrical activity. If they find no heart problem, stress or anxiety may be behind it, and the tips above may help.

Many times, it can feel like your heart is racing for no reason. But your body could be reacting to subtle stress signals or low-lying anxiety. Poor sleep, dehydration, low blood sugar, and even scrolling through overwhelming news can all tell your nervous system to go into high alert.

Recent findings suggest that it can also happen when your system’s on edge, and as a result, it doesn’t take much to push it over. When this happens, it is usually just your body trying to protect you.

Mindfulness can help lower your heart rate. Techniques like breathwork, grounding, and body scans have been shown to activate your parasympathetic nervous system, which slows your heart rate and helps regulate stress responses.

Practicing mindfulness can be as simple as noticing your feet on the ground or taking a few deep breaths after you brush your teeth. Little moments like this can help remind your body that it’s not in danger.

In a recent development, A good way to decrease your heart rate is to slow your breathing, especially your exhale. This signals safety to your nervous system. Other useful tools are:.

Practicing the 5–4–3–2–1 technique by naming five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste.

Placing a hand over your chest to create a sense of connection and calm.

Changing your body position by uncrossing your legs and relaxing your shoulders.

Getting some fresh air by going for a brief walk.

Engaging your senses by holding something cold.

Anxiety and elevated heart rate often reinforce each other. This is because when your brain senses a threat, your heart races. Then your racing heart convinces your brain that something must be wrong. But the good news is that lowering your heart rate can help disrupt this cycle.

Some ways to do this are slowing your breathing, moving gently, and bringing your attention back to your body. All of these actions can create just enough space for your thoughts to soften.

According to recent reports, an occasional spike during rest, especially when you’re anxious or overtired, is usually not dangerous. But if your resting heart rate is consistently elevated, it could be worth talking to a healthcare provider. Chronic stress, certain medications, and underlying conditions could be playing a role.

Recent findings suggest that with that stated, bodies do fluctuate. So pay more attention to the broader pattern of how often it happens and what might be triggering it.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

How to reduce screen time and improve your digital well-being

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once a week, your phone sends you a screen time report.
  • Screen time adds up fast when work emails and news alerts share a device with your group chats and favorite shows.
  • Recent findings suggest that conventional wisdom might say “just put the phone down.” But you don’t have to completely give up screens to feel more in control of how you use them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Once a week, your phone sends you a screen time report. You wince at the number, then swipe it away with the same thumb you were scrolling with.

Screen time adds up fast when work emails and news alerts share a device with your group chats and favorite shows. By evening, you can feel worn out even if the day wasn’t particularly busy.

Recent findings suggest that conventional wisdom might say “just put the phone down.” But you don’t have to completely give up screens to feel more in control of how you use them. A few small tweaks to your daily routine are a good place to start. Below, you’ll find some realistic ways to cut back, plus a look at why it can feel so hard to put your phone down.

There's no set amount of time that counts as too much. What matters more is how your screen use affects you. Signs worth noticing include strained eyes, restless sleep, reaching for your phone out of habit, and feeling worse after scrolling. If any of these sound familiar, the tips below may help.

💙 Not sure if this sounds like you? Check out these five signs you might be online too much.

In a recent development, if “one more video” keeps turning into one more hour, you’re in good tech giant. Many apps are designed to keep you scrolling, so you’ll need more than willpower to cut back. Start with one or two tips that feel doable right now. You can come back to the rest later.

Bright colors can make apps harder to put down, and notification badges and thumbnails are built to draw you in. Switching your screen to black and white takes away some of that appeal, which can make scrolling feel less rewarding.

According to recent reports, try: Search “grayscale” or “color filters” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under Accessibility or Well-Being.

Grayscale may look odd for a day or two. Some people keep it on all day, and others only turn it on in the evening to wind down. You can turn it off whenever you need to, like when you’re using maps or looking at photos.

💙 Listen to the Build Healthier Phone Habits series with Dr. Aditi Nerurkar on Calm.

Industry observers note that time can slip by while you scroll. Set a daily limit on your one or two most-used apps, and your phone will nudge you when you reach it.

In a recent development, try: Search “app limits” or “app timers” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under screen time.

Start with a limit slightly below how much you use those apps now, then lower it gradually. Smaller steps are often more sustainable than cutting back all at once.

Industry observers note that notifications like news alerts, app promos, social likes, and game reminders mostly add noise. Keep the ones you rely on, such as texts, calls, and reminders, and turn off the rest.

Try: Search “notifications” in your device settings, then toggle off the alerts you don’t need, starting with the apps that send the most.

Constant check-ins can keep you glued to your screens all day. Pick a few set times to go through your messages, emails, and feeds.

Try: Limit your check-ins to lunchtime and after work, and keep your personal devices out of reach in between.

In a recent development, before you open your phone, take one slow breath and ask yourself why you’re reaching for it. If the answer is just habit, that brief pause may be enough to snap you out of autopilot.

Try: Breathe in for four counts and out for six, then see if you still want to unlock your phone.

💙 Discover 10 types of breathing exercises you can try anytime, anywhere.

When you feel the urge to pick up your phone, try turning to an offline activity instead. Keep an activity you enjoy within reach, like a book on the couch or a sketchpad on the table.

Industry observers note that 💙 Want to work on the habit before the urge hits? Explore Tame Your Scrolling Habit with Rose Nisker on Calm.

Choose one or two spots to keep screen-free, such as the dinner table or your bedroom. A clear boundary often works better than a vague promise to use screens less. These zones also give you room to be more present, like during a family meal or your evening wind-down.

Try: Place your phone in a dedicated spot, like a basket by the door. If you share a home, invite everyone to join.

💙 Not ready to go phone-free at night? Tune in to Sleeping with Your Phone with Dr. Matthew Walker on Calm.

Pick a cutoff time for all your screens, such as 30 minutes before bed, and stick to it as best you can. Late-night screen use can keep your mind active and make it harder to fall asleep.

If you usually watch a TV show before bed, choose one episode and turn off autoplay.

Sources indicate that try: Schedule a nightly reminder for your cutoff. Swap your screen time for a calming activity, like journaling or a short meditation.

💙 Press play on the Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

A few common app features can keep you hooked:.

Infinite scroll: Upcoming posts keep loading, so you never reach a natural stopping point.

Autoplay: The next video or episode starts on its own, which keeps you watching unless you stop it.

Unpredictable notifications: Each message or like feels like a small reward, and not knowing when the next one will pop up keeps you checking.

Your emotions play a part too. A screen can be a quick escape when you’re stressed or putting something off. It can bring relief in the moment, even if you feel more drained afterward.

💙 If your screen time has been weighing on your mood, read our guide on what to do if technology is impacting your mental health.

If you want to cut back on screen time without giving up after a few days, start small. Choose one change, like keeping your phone off the dinner table, and give yourself time to adjust before you make another tweak to your routine. If you slip back into old habits, you can always start again the next day.

Industry observers note that to set screen time limits that stick, build them into your routine so you don’t have to rely on willpower in the moment. You could use an app timer or set aside a screen-free time each day, like the first half hour after you wake up.

There isn’t a daily screen time limit that works for every adult. If you’d like to use screens less, a good starting point is a limit slightly below your current daily average, and you can lower that limit gradually as you get used to it.

How you spend your screen time matters just as much. An hour on a video call with a friend often leaves you feeling better than an hour of doomscrolling.

You can reduce your screen time at night by setting a cutoff time before bed and charging your phone across the room. Swap your late-night scroll for a book or a short meditation to help you relax before sleep.

To help your family reduce screen time together, make it a shared initiative. You could agree on screen-free times, such as during meals or the first hour after school or work. Try leading by example, rather than telling your kids or partner what to do.

In a recent development, no, you don’t have to quit screens completely to feel better. Technology connects you to the people and things you care about. You can cut back on the screen use that leaves you feeling worse, like aimless scrolling, and keep what you value.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

How to Deal With the Grief of an Aging Body

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.
  • It has been revealed that unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there.
  • This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.

It has been revealed that unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there. It may feel impossible to live well unless you do.

This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).

Recent global estimates suggest one in five people are right now experiencing chronic pain. The most prevalent chronic pain reported by adults ages 75 and over includes low back pain and migraine, while tension-type headaches are more often experienced by younger adults. Chronic illness (diabetes, heart disease, and other mid-to-late-life diagnoses) affects about three-quarters of the world population.

In a recent development, despite how common chronic illness is worldwide, the nuances of navigating a changing body are not often discussed. It’s time for an honest, evidence-based conversation about what it means to navigate chronic pain and illness, aging and transforming identity post-diagnosis, and how to grieve this loss and maintain meaning through these changes.

Research suggest that those with internalized stigma of chronic illness are more preoccupied with how their illness detracts from their view of themselves, and also have a greater tendency to overlook positive aspects of life with a chronic illness.

According to recent reports, psychologists have observed how preoccupation with illness or pain is often accompanied by other grief behaviors. A 2025 study explored how Danish chronic illness patients navigated loss and growth. The study found that many with chronic illness find themselves mourning the life that they thought they would have, often leading to loss of motivation and joy in everyday life.

The perception of losing the life they had once envisioned is often accompanied by a focus on getting back to the “before illness” version of themselves as people struggle to accept how their body has changed, perhaps in how it looks but definitely in how it feels.

These changes and associated feelings of loss often permeate a person’s sense of identity, as well as their perceived roles within social relationships. Many report a fear of burdening others, especially loved ones, often describing feelings of guilt that “others have it worse than I do.” This is where internalized stigma festers.

Some people have also described feelings of anger, isolation, shame, and exhaustion accompanying sadness. Meanwhile, others have expressed frustration over a gradual loss rather than a “clean break,” accompanied by the inability to find closure.

Sources indicate that first, it’s vital to understand why accepting this continuous loss feels so impossible. Theories of control in psychology state that humans desire control or the ability to achieve a desired outcome according to our own standards.

The best and most enduring of our articles, podcasts, and videos about getting older.

Industry observers note that when that ability is seen as stripped away, people are more likely to experience negative mental health symptoms, like anxiety, depression, and even grief. Specifically, feelings of diminished perceived control (subjective belief about our ability to achieve desired outcomes) occur when we face continuous roadblocks to living our desired life because of chronic illness.

In a recent development, one of the major consequences of loss and major life change is that it can disrupt meaning and challenge identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future. At a time when people feel there is little they can control, psychologist Robert Neimeyer’s Meaning Reconstruction Theory poses the questions: “How do I move forward?” and “What matters most?”.

In a recent development, while the original theory was proposed as an approach to coping with the loss of a loved one, the process is somewhat similar to grieving the close ally that is your body. This theory approaches grief by making sense of the loss and finding ways to rebuild a sense of purpose in a changed life (and body).

To answer relevant questions about how to move forward with chronic illness, two ongoing approaches are needed: integrating the loss and recentering purpose and meaning.

Integrating the loss may look like processing significant bodily losses in therapy, finding trusted loved ones to talk about the loss with, and focusing on being realistic about your current body without judgment.

Second, recentering purpose during this major life change involves understanding your why: why is this loss so significant to you, why does it hurt? Maybe it’s because you love hiking in the mountains and a latest diagnosis with arthritis feels like the end of this joy. Part of rebuilding meaning is finding new approaches to fulfilling this purpose—perhaps hiking may look different, but nature can be accessed and loved with chronic illness present.

It has been revealed that rebuilding meaning might also look like making meaning from this loss: What has this change taught you about yourself, about the impact you can make? Approaching present and future with this perspective helps process grief in a more protective way.

In a recent development, living with chronic pain, illness, and the changes that come with aging often involves grieving physical loss, but also shifts in purpose, relationships, identity, and future prepares. While these changes challenge our perceived control and purpose, the Meaning Reconstruction Theory suggests that acceptance and growth comes with integrating loss and rebuilding purpose alongside these changes.

Although the present is different than anticipated, fulfillment is still possible with your current body.
