A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area.

Wernicke’s area, located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the human brain, has long been considered essential for understanding speech. However, damage to this region also disrupts the ability to produce speech, creating a long-standing puzzle in neuroscience. Traditional explanations propose that this area primarily supports speech production indirectly by monitoring sounds during speaking. However, it remains unclear whether this region plays a more direct role in generating speech itself, and if so, what kind of information it represents: sounds, movements, or even properties of whole words. Resolving this question is critical for understanding how the brain constructs language and for developing technologies to restore speech in individuals who have lost it.

According to recent reports, addressing this question requires probing the human brain at multiple scales with both correlational and causal methods. We combined several complementary approaches, including high-resolution direct recordings of neural populations and single neurons during speaking and listening, electrical stimulation of specific brain regions to test causality, and analysis of patients with localized brain lesions. Across these methods, participants performed a variety of speaking and listening tasks ranging from naturalistic speech to single word repetition, providing a detailed and holistic view of the role of the posterior temporal lobe in generating upcoming speech.

It has been revealed that we identified a specific subregion within individual participants’ Wernicke’s area—the left posterior superior temporal gyrus—that becomes active before speech begins. This early activity precedes word onsets in continuous speech rather than reflecting feedback from hearing one’s own voice. Brain stimulation and lesion analyses showed that disrupting this region causes errors in speech production, confirming its causal role.

Sources indicate that detailed analyses revealed that this region encodes properties of entire words, such as their length and frequency, rather than individual sounds or motor movements. This is distinct from neighboring brain regions that encode auditory feedback and do so by representing lower-level features such as articulation or sound.

Timing analyses indicated that activity in this region occurs earlier than in motor areas responsible for controlling speech muscles, placing it at the start of the speech production process. Recordings from individual neurons further confirmed that cells in this region respond before speech production, respond selectively to specific words, and are active during both speaking and listening.

Finally, in people unable to speak due to paralysis, signals from this region could be used to decode both intended and perceived speech, demonstrating its potential for multimodal brain-computer interface technologies aimed at restoring communication.

Recent findings suggest that this work identifies a specialized region within Wernicke’s area that generates word-level representations before speech is produced. Rather than serving primarily as a center for speech perception, this region acts as an early stage in the production process, organizing upcoming words before they are translated into motor commands. These findings resolve a long-standing paradox about Wernicke’s area and provide a unified framework for understanding how the brain links language comprehension and production. They also highlight a promising target for future neuroprosthetic devices aimed at restoring speech in individuals with communication impairments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks of sleep tracking linked higher levels of one vitamin to longer, more consistent sleep.

Two weeks of sleep tracking linked higher levels of one vitamin to longer, more consistent sleep.

People with higher vitamin D levels tend to sleep longer and have more consistent sleep patterns.

Those with higher levels also tend to spend a greater proportion of their time in bed asleep.

One proposed explanation involves melatonin, the hormone that helps signal when it is time to sleep.

The findings suggest that vitamin D status and sleep may be connected through other biological processes or shared everyday habits.

The research involved almost 80 generally healthy adults aged 18 to 45, recruited from the University of Delaware and the surrounding area.

Participants wore wrist monitors for two weeks, allowing researchers to estimate their sleep duration and timing.

Blood tests measured vitamin D levels, while urine samples provided an indicator of overnight melatonin production.

Before statistical adjustments, people whose vitamin D levels were 10 ng/mL higher slept around 12 minutes longer per night.

The association with longer sleep remained across the adjusted analyses, although several other links weakened.

Because the research was observational, it cannot establish whether increasing vitamin D improves sleep.

Sleep follows an internal rhythm that repeats roughly every 24 hours.

Light reaching the eyes helps the brain keep this rhythm aligned with the cycle of day and night.

As darkness falls, the brain normally increases its release of melatonin, helping the body prepare for sleep.

Bright artificial light late in the evening can interfere with this process and delay that signal.

Time spent outdoors and physical activity can also influence these rhythms.

Sunlight has another role in the body, allowing exposed skin to produce vitamin D.

People who spend little time outside may have more difficulty obtaining enough of the vitamin.

Food provides another source, particularly oily fish such as salmon and mackerel, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Previous research offers some evidence that vitamin D supplements may improve how people rate their sleep quality (Abboud, 2022).

A review brought together 19 intervention studies, although only three trials could be combined in its main statistical analysis.

Those trials found improvements in questionnaire scores after supplementation, but participants included people with fibromyalgia and those receiving methadone treatment.

Results for sleep duration and specific sleep disorders were less consistent, leaving questions about who might benefit and which aspects of sleep could change.

The study was published in the journal SLEEP Advances (D’Agata et al., 2025).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women.
  • Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women. The findings suggest that internalized beauty standards reshape how the brain regulates and evaluates objectifying media.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.

Over time, repeated exposure to objectifying imagery can lead individuals to internalize an observer’s gaze, a psychological phenomenon known as self-objectification, in which a person habitually monitors and evaluates their own body from an outsider’s perspective.

While behavioral studies have established that self-objectification heightens sensitivity to media portrayals, precisely how a woman’s self-perception alters the underlying neural circuitry that evaluates sexualized visuals has remained unclear.

In a study published today in eNeuro, a research team led by Zhennan Liu at Shanghai Normal University and Haoyue Qian at the Chinese Academy of Sciences investigated how individual differences in self-objectification shape both subjective beauty judgments and brain responses to sexualized imagery.

In a recent development, the investigators recruited 60 healthy cisgender heterosexual female participants with an average age of approximately 20 years. First, the team assessed each participant’s baseline level of self-objectification using a validated psychological scale measuring how strongly individuals prioritize external appearance over internal bodily competence.

Next, participants viewed and rated a series of photographs categorized by the researchers as either:.

While participants across the board rated the sexualized photographs as more attractive than the non-sexualized images, women with higher self-objectification scores assigned significantly higher attractiveness ratings to the sexualized visuals.

When the team examined the accompanying brain activity, they uncovered a striking neural signature: women who scored higher on self-objectification exhibited dampened neural activity in brain regions involved in aesthetic judgment while assessing sexualized images.

Rather than heightened analytical engagement, this reduced activation suggests an altered regulatory or automatic evaluative response when processing culturally idealized, objectifying imagery.

“Differences between individuals [in this study] may come from how their brains regulate and evaluate the attractiveness of these images,” explained Qian.

By connecting self-objectification to measurable shifts in aesthetic evaluation circuitry, the study illustrates how internalized social standards leave a functional footprint on visual and emotional processing.

Looking ahead, the researchers aim to move beyond observational associations to test whether psychological training can buffer the brain against objectifying media.

“We want to test whether experimentally training or manipulating regulation strategies (e.g., cognitive reappraisal) can change how women respond to and rate sexualized images,” Qian remarked. “This will help move the work from association toward causal and intervention-relevant questions.”.

What is “self-objectification,” and how did researchers measure it?

Self-objectification is the tendency to view and judge one’s own body primarily from an outside observer’s perspective, prioritizing physical appearance over internal physical capabilities. Researchers measured this trait using a validated psychological questionnaire before participants viewed media images.

How did self-objectification affect brain responses to sexualized images?

Women with higher self-objectification scores rated sexualized images of women as significantly more attractive than peers with lower scores, and demonstrated dampened brain activity in regions responsible for aesthetic judgment, indicating differences in how their brains regulate and evaluate beauty standards.

Could psychological strategies change how the brain reacts to objectifying media?

Researchers hope to test whether training cognitive regulation techniques, such as cognitive reappraisal, which helps people consciously reframe how they interpret visual stimuli, can modify brain activity and reduce vulnerability to sexualized media representations.

Trait Self-Objectification Modulates Attractiveness-Regulating Neural Activity in Sexual Objectification Processing: An ERP Study.

According to recent reports, contemporary mass media frequently emphasize women’s sexual attractiveness, thereby perpetuating sexual objectification and exacerbating mental distress. Trait self-objectification is presumed to be a risk factor for these adverse outcomes; however, the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying individuals’ responses to sexual objectification remain poorly understood.

It has been revealed that the present study examined how trait self-objectification modulates behavioral and electrophysiological responses to sexualized female images. Behaviorally, sexualized portrayals of women increased attractiveness ratings, and this enhancement was further modulated by individual levels of trait self-objectification. Neurally, processing sexualized female images evoked a set of ERPs indexing early neurocognitive processes, including perception-related N170 and EPN, and attention-related P200.

Sources indicate that distinct later neural responses were also identified, including the emotion-related centro-parietal LPP and the regulation-related frontal LPP (f-LPP). Among these sexual objectification-related ERP components, only the f-LPP was modulated by trait self-objectification.

Furthermore, follow-up analyses revealed that the degree to which trait self-objectification increased individuals’ attractiveness ratings of sexualized images was associated with their reduced f-LPP activity.

Collectively, these findings suggest that trait self-objectification modulates the processing of sexually objectifying stimuli by altering neurocognitive processes underlying attractiveness regulation, highlighting the importance of this regulatory mechanism in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

Recent findings suggest that the cultural emphasis on women’s sexual attractiveness perpetuates sexual objectification, which is associated with adverse mental health outcomes. Trait self-objectification may modulate these outcomes, yet its relationship with the processing of sexual objectification remains unclear. This study found that trait self-objectification shapes attractiveness ratings during sexual objectification processing.

According to recent reports, although sexualized images elicited multiple neurocognitive components—N170 and EPN (perception-related), P200 (attention-related), cp-LPP (emotion-related), and f-LPP (regulation-related)—individual differences in trait self-objectification were selectively associated with f-LPP activity. These findings highlight the potential role of attractiveness-related regulatory processing in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

#91891. For How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

For How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice.
  • Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.
  • In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice. Many had never meditated, while others had dabbled years before.

Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.

In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.

Now, you might expect that longer meditations would deliver greater benefits. After all, we’re conditioned to believe that more is better—especially when it comes to self-improvement. But this research and many other studies find that more minutes don’t necessarily mean more benefit: Shorter practices can work just as well—and sometimes better—while consistency may matter more than duration.

In this first study, each participant attended four 25-minute sessions over two weeks. In every session, the time not spent on audio-guided mindfulness-of-breath practice was filled by Bryson’s eloquence. To ensure the results reflected only the study activities, participants were asked to avoid any formal mindfulness practices outside these sessions.

After those two weeks, the five-minute meditators actually highlighted greater improvements in stress and mindful awareness (the tendency to stay present in daily life with less judgement) than the 20-minute group. Even depression and anxiety improved just as much—if not more.

Was the extra time with Bryson the magic ingredient for those five-minute meditators? The control group, who luxuriated in 25 uninterrupted minutes of his charm, demonstrated no meaningful improvement. So while his voice may soothe, it wasn’t what moved the needle.

One five-minute meditator put it this way: “I always thought that to do mindfulness, I’d need a long time to dedicate to this, which seemed too challenging to even start. But I’ve learned that five minutes can help!” In contrast, a 20-minute participant admitted, “I think a shorter one would be better for me to learn mindfulness.”.

There’s more. The facilitator observed that participants in the 20-minute meditation sessions more often fidgeted, shifted in their seats, and peeked through half-closed eyes, as if tranquility were just out of reach. Meanwhile, the five-minute meditators appeared more at ease and less prone to these signs of discomfort. Five of them even requested recordings to continue at home. The 20-minute group? Not a single request. For these beginners, less really did seem to be more.

Now, before you dash off to cancel that meditation retreat, remember that this study focused on people with little to no meditation experience. So if you’re a seasoned meditator, those longer sessions might still pack more punch for you, as we’ll explore later. And both the five-minute and 20-minute groups demonstrated improvements in mindful awareness, depression, anxiety, and stress compared to the control group. The five-minute meditators just improved more when it came to mindful awareness and stress.

The takeaway? For beginners, a quick dip into mindfulness might be more refreshing than a long soak.

You might be wondering, Isn’t this just one study? Could it be a fluke? But multiple randomized controlled trials have explored how the length of meditation shapes its impact.

I join Christine Carter, Ph.D, in a webinar next week to talk about my book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick.

In a recent development, in the largest of these studies, researchers recruited 372 adults online—about half of them new to meditation—to see how the “dose” of mindfulness meditation affected mindful awareness and emotional well-being. Participants were randomly sorted into one of four groups: Some meditated for 10 minutes, others for 20, and the rest listened to a 10- or 20-minute National Geographic article on sequoia trees. (Because nothing soothes stress like a deep dive into bark thickness.).

Industry observers note that what did the researchers find? The 10-minute meditators indicated greater improvements in mindful awareness than those who listened to the 10-minute sequoia lecture. Surprisingly, the 20-minute meditation group didn’t outperform any group—not even the tree enthusiasts. In fact, the 10-minute group showed slightly greater improvements in mindful awareness than the 20-minute meditators, although the difference wasn’t statistically significant, meaning it could have occurred by chance. Still, it suggests that for boosting mindful awareness right after practice, 10 minutes might be at least as effective as 20.

But that was just one session. What happens with consistent practice? In another study, 77 college students were randomly assigned to meditate daily for 10 or 20 minutes. After two weeks, both groups showed similar improvements in stress and, again, mindful awareness. But those assigned to the 20-minute group experienced a slightly greater boost in self-compassion, the skill of meeting your own struggles with the kindness you’d offer a dear friend.

So if you’ve poured hours into longer meditations, you can rest easy—it wasn’t for nothing. The evidence suggests that whether your sessions are short or sustained, they can offer meaningful benefits.

Another notable finding is that the 10-minute group practiced more consistently, logging about 82 minutes total. The 20-minute group missed more days and didn’t always finish, ending up with just 103. Double the goal, barely a quarter more practice.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever tried meditating, you might be nodding along. Some sessions are bliss, while others are a tug-of-war with time. Maybe you’ve battled that nagging frustration, trying to keep your mind steady for more than a fleeting moment. Or felt the magnetic pull of distraction, your mind wandering just when you need it to stay put. As the minutes crawl, doubt can creep in: Am I even doing this right? Is it worth it? These tough moments can teach you a lot, but they can also make meditation feel intimidating—and make you less likely to stick with it, especially when you’re just starting out. Another study looked at even longer sessions, comparing 10 minutes of meditation to 30 minutes. This experiment split 161 adults into four groups: 10 or 30 minutes of daily sitting meditation, or the same amount of mindful movement. The mindful movement was a stretching practice that brings mindful awareness into motion—less stillness, same presence.

According to recent reports, after two weeks, everyone saw benefits: Mindful awareness increased, well-being improved, and distress levels dropped. But there were no significant differences among the groups. Whether they meditated for 10 minutes or 30, sitting or moving, all the groups seemed to benefit equally.

So, here’s the bottom line: One study found that longer sessions more strongly boosted self-compassion. Another highlighted that shorter ones more effectively reduced stress. But across studies, most of the key benefits—mindful awareness, mental health, well-being—weren’t tied to how long people practiced.

According to recent reports, why? Because as we’ll keep exploring, the nervous system learns through repetition, not duration. It’s consistency that reshapes patterns. Not heroic efforts once in a while, but showing up, again and again, however you can.

Sources indicate that the benefits of consistency over length show up in observational studies, too, where people choose how often and how long to meditate. While observational studies can’t pin down cause and effect, they offer a richer view of how shorter practices play out in the real world.

According to recent reports, imagine it’s early morning. You reach for your phone and open Insight Timer, a free meditation app. Before your meditation, it asks, “How are you today?” You tap an icon—maybe “OK,” maybe “great”—capturing a snapshot of your mood in seconds.

Now imagine doing this regularly, for 14 months straight. That’s exactly what 10,409 people from 103 countries did in a groundbreaking study. Many were new to meditation, using the app to track their emotional ups and downs in real time. It’s like taking your emotional temperature—not with a thermometer, but with a single tap that sums up how you feel.

The findings? Consistency (four to seven days a week)—not duration—was the strongest predictor of better mood, resilience, and equanimity, the ability to stay cool under pressure. Think of it like watering a plant: A little each week keeps it happy and growing. Forget all month and drown it after four weeks? It wilts anyway.

In a recent development, for beginners in the Insight Timer study, short sessions—five to 10 minutes—outshone longer ones in improving mood over time. But after 20 sessions? Longer practices—21 to 30 minutes—began to take the lead in mood improvement. It’s like your brain needs to build its meditation muscles before longer sessions feel better than short ones—like a marathon that only gives you the high once you’ve earned it.

But do shorter sessions lose their impact as you gain experience? Not at all. They might just become your secret weapon. After 80 sessions, shorter practices make a late-game comeback, boosting equanimity and showing that even seasoned meditators can benefit from briefer sessions.

Sources indicate that the idea that consistency beats duration is backed by a meta-analysis challenging the belief that longer equals better. Think of a meta-analysis as a “study of studies,” combining data from multiple research papers to uncover clearer, substantial-picture insights.

Recent findings suggest that when researchers analyzed 203 randomized controlled trials totaling 15,971 participants, they found no association between meditation session length and better outcomes. In fact, a trend emerged in favor of shorter practices for reducing depression symptoms, although it wasn’t statistically significant. Still, shorter sessions were at least as effective as longer ones, calling into question the assumption that more minutes always mean more benefits. So what’s the takeaway? When you’re starting out, don’t sweat the long stuff. Quick sessions might do more to lift your mood early on. As you settle in, longer practices might bring deeper emotional gains. But even if you’re a pro, short sessions don’t lose their value—they just shift their superpower, helping you stay steady when life throws you curveballs. Different strengths, different stages. And who doesn’t love a shortcut that actually works?

Eli Susman, Ph.D., is a UC Berkeley-trained psychologist, former Harvard researcher, and author of Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, forthcoming in 22 languages.

Does Working Harder Make Learning Fun?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A new psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable.
  • In a recent development, parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it.
  • Yet a newly introduced psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A new psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable. Three experiments reveal that while cognitive effort improves comprehension, it does not spark curiosity or enjoyment, instead, preexisting interest motivates students to engage in the first place.

In a recent development, parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it. Behind this common wisdom lies an intuitive assumption that sustained cognitive effort naturally blossoms into curiosity and intrinsic motivation.

Yet a newly introduced psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.

According to recent reports, published in Acta Psychologica, the study demonstrates that forcing effort improves basic comprehension, but it does not make dry or unappealing material more interesting. Instead, genuine interest and liking come first—serving as the psychological spark that motivates learners to invest cognitive effort voluntarily.

Industry observers note that “I’m curious if a student is made to work harder, does that bring the same benefits as effort they choose to give,” asked Yimeng Jin, a doctoral student at Kyushu University’s Graduate School of Systems Life Sciences and first author of the study. “It matters because many learning environments rely on required effort, such as assignments, on the assumption that more effort is always better.”.

To disentangle voluntary motivation from mandatory mental exertion, Jin and senior author Professor Johan Lauwereyns at Kyushu University’s Faculty of Arts and Science conducted three behavioral experiments involving 110 university students.

Participants read pairs of seemingly unrelated sentences and decided whether they wanted to construct an explanation connecting them. By tracking participants’ initial choices, task completion, and time spent, the team isolated two distinct components of learning: willingness to engage and cognitive effort invested.

Across the three experimental phases, a clear cognitive pattern emerged:.

Sources indicate that “Interestingly, participants who were required to explain spent more time on the task than those who chose to do so,” Jin noted. “Perhaps they initially skipped it because the sentences were harder to understand, so they needed more time to make sense of them. It’s a bit like struggling through homework in a subject you don’t enjoy. Together, the experiments suggest that effort can help people make sense of information, while interest is more closely linked to their willingness to engage.”.

While the researchers caution that short laboratory reading tasks among university students differ from long-term classroom learning in younger children, the findings carry broad implications for how educators, parents, and communicators design learning environments. Rather than relying solely on mandatory drill work to manufacture enthusiasm, sparking authentic curiosity first may unlock deeper, faster comprehension.

Recent findings suggest that “The findings have implications far outside education. The connection between engagement and effort is key whenever our understanding depends on reading texts,” concluded Lauwereyns.

Does working harder on a subject automatically make it more enjoyable?

No. Researchers at Kyushu University found that while putting in cognitive effort helps students better understand difficult material, it does not increase their interest in or enjoyment of the subject.

What actually motivates students to put effort into learning?

Sources indicate that the experiments revealed that preexisting interest and liking come first. When students already find a topic intriguing, they are far more willing to engage voluntarily, and they comprehend the material more efficiently than when forced to work through topics they want to skip.

What happens when students are forced to work on material they don’t find interesting?

When participants were required to explain material they initially chose to skip, they spent significantly more time struggling with the task, gained less comprehension compared to voluntary effort, and indicated no increase in enjoyment.

Effort enhances understanding, while appreciation drives engagement in Cross-sentence semantic processing.

According to recent reports, comprehensive reading requires active semantic processing, going beyond explicitly stated information to construct connections and meaning. Building on discourse coherence theory, Reader-Response Theory and insights from Language Poetry, the present research investigates how active engagement and cognitive effort shape semantic processing.

We propose that evaluative dimensions central to aesthetic appreciation, namely understanding, interest, and liking, also play key roles in semantic processing.

To examine these processes, we developed a novel cross-sentence elaboration paradigm using unconnected, randomly paired sentences that create semantic gaps and encourage reader-driven meaning construction.

Recent findings suggest that in Experiment 1, participants could voluntarily invest effort by thinking aloud during elaboration. Results indicated greater volitional engagement was associated with higher levels of understanding, interest, and appreciation.

Experiment 2 dissociated willingness to engage from actual effort, revealing that appreciation predicted participants’ willingness to invest further effort, whereas additional completed effort did not consistently increase appreciation.

Experiment 3 examined forced effort, showing that externally imposed effort enhanced semantic understanding but did not consistently increase appreciation, highlighting the distinct roles of volitional and imposed effort.

An integrated 2 × 2 analysis of Experiments 2 and 3 showed that active engagement and cognitive effort made distinct, interactive contributions to evaluation and processing time, with completed cognitive effort more reliably predicting accurate recognition memory and active engagement more closely tied to memory for the processing context.

Together, these findings clarify the interplay between engagement, effort, understanding, and appreciation, offering new insights into the cognitive dynamics of active meaning construction in semantic processing.

Latest Update: High-Speed Nanoscale Brain Imaging Uncovers Hidden Synapses

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers dramatically accelerated electron tomography to map large volumes of brain tissue at 15-nanometer 3D resolution.
  • It has been revealed that to understand how billions of neurons orchestrate thoughts, memories, and movement, neuroscientists construct connectomes, detailed wiring diagrams mapping how brain cells connect and communicate.
  • As a result, even the most ambitious brain wiring maps have routinely missed ultra-fine cellular architectures, including electrical synapses (also called gap junctions), microscopic channels that enable direct, near-instantaneous electrical communication between adjacent neurons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers dramatically accelerated electron tomography to map large volumes of brain tissue at 15-nanometer 3D resolution. The breakthrough captures fine neural structures missed by conventional connectomes, including rapid-fire electrical synapses and uncharacterized protrusions where neurons appear to “nibble” neighboring glial cells.

It has been revealed that to understand how billions of neurons orchestrate thoughts, memories, and movement, neuroscientists construct connectomes, detailed wiring diagrams mapping how brain cells connect and communicate. While macro-scale MRI scans chart major white-matter highways and standard electron microscopy traces individual chemical synapses, scaling up to large tissue volumes has historically forced a difficult compromise: sacrificing nanoscale structural detail for imaging speed.

As a result, even the most ambitious brain wiring maps have routinely missed ultra-fine cellular architectures, including electrical synapses (also called gap junctions), microscopic channels that enable direct, near-instantaneous electrical communication between adjacent neurons.

Now, in a study published November 19 in Nature Methods, researchers at Harvard Medical School (HMS) and the University of California San Diego have overcome that bottleneck by supercharging electron tomography—a 3D imaging technique that reconstructs nanoscale architecture by tilting tissue samples and capturing views from multiple angles.

Industry observers note that led by co-senior authors Dr. Wei-Chung Allen Lee (associate professor of neurobiology at HMS and associate professor of neurology at Boston Children’s Hospital) and Dr. Mark Ellisman (UC San Diego), alongside co-first authors Dr. Aaron T. Kuan and Dr. Sébastien Phan, the team demonstrated that large blocks of brain tissue can be mapped in exquisite 3D nanoscale detail without prohibitive imaging times.

In a recent development, conventional electron tomography is painstakingly slow because it typically requires capturing hundreds of tilted images across razor-thin tissue slices. By refining image acquisition and computational reconstruction, Lee, Ellisman, and colleagues discovered they could cut the required number of images by roughly 50-fold while imaging tissue sections 20 times thicker than standard electron microscopy protocols, preserving an extraordinary 3D resolution of 15 nanometers or finer.

“We can now see brain structures that we haven’t been able to see before in connectomics data,” explained Lee. “We hope this work will help us understand how nervous systems are built; what changes with age; and what goes awry in neurodevelopmental, cognitive, and neurodegenerative disorders.”.

When the researchers applied their high-speed tomography pipeline to tissue from the mouse cerebellum, the 3D reconstructions revealed both long-sought neural connections and surprising cellular behaviors:.

“We’re seeing uncharacterized structures, suggesting that neurons are ‘nibbling’ their neighboring cells,” Lee noted.

In addition, the researchers traced delicate nerve fibers continuously through the thick 3D tissue block right down to their exact synaptic contact points with target neurons.

While scaling this accelerated tomography workflow to map an entire mammalian brain will require automated tissue-handling robotics, the breakthrough bridges a critical resolution gap in modern connectomics—equipping neuroscientists to examine how fine electrical and glial-neuronal connections form in early life and break down in brain disease.

Why do traditional brain wiring maps (connectomes) miss certain structures?

Mapping large volumes of brain tissue at high speed usually forces scientists to sacrifice ultra-fine resolution. As a result, critical microscopic features, such as tiny electrical synapses (gap junctions) that connect neurons directly, often blur out or go undetected in large-scale datasets.

How did researchers speed up nanoscale 3D brain imaging?

The team optimized electron tomography so that it requires about 50 times fewer multi-angle images on tissue slices 20 times thicker than usual, while still maintaining a 3D resolution of 15 nanometers or finer.

What surprising new structures did they see in the brain tissue?

Alongside hard-to-see electrical synapses in the mouse cerebellum, the researchers discovered tiny protrusions between neurons and neighboring support cells (glia), suggesting that neurons physically “nibble” or take up material from adjacent cells.

Funding: This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants RF1MH129261, U01NS142013, and K99EB032217), with startup support to Kuan from the Yale School of Medicine Department of Neuroscience and Wu Tsai Institute.

Industry observers note that harvard University filed a patent application regarding GridTape (WO2017184621A1) on behalf of inventors, including Lee, and negotiated licensing agreements with interested partners. All other authors have no competing interests.

Scalable electron tomography for connectomics.

We demonstrate limited-tilt, serial-section electron tomography (ET), which can non-destructively map brain circuits over large 3D volumes and provide high-resolution, supramolecular details within subvolumes of interest.

Here we show accelerated ET imaging of semi-thick sections ( >500 nm) from the mouse cerebellar cortex, with 3D resolution <15 nm and machine learning-based image augmentation, providing the capacity to resolve key features of neuronal circuits including chemical synapses, endocytic structures and gap junctions.

Furthermore, we systematically assess how imaging parameters affect image quality and speed to enable connectomic-scale projects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An international consortium has created personalized biophysical “digital brain twins” for 6,986 individuals across 16 countries to uncover how aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and environmental conditions shape neural dynamics. The computational models simulate excitation-inhibition balance across 90 connected brain regions, revealing distinct mechanistic signatures for Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal degeneration, and environmental exposures ranging from air pollution to democratic governance.

Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an invaluable window into the living human brain, yet it records only indirect proxies of neural activity, typically relying on group averages that obscure individual variation and say little about the underlying cellular mechanisms driving those signals.

It has been revealed that now, an international research team led by corresponding author Dr. Agustín Ibáñez (Scientific Director of BrainLat at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, strategic director of core scientific assets at the BarcelonaBeta Brain Research Center, and faculty at the Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin) and first author Dr. Rubén Herzog (BrainLat and Distinguished Professor at the University of the Balearic Islands) has transformed static brain scans into dynamic, personalized virtual laboratories.

Published today in Nature Biomedical Engineering, the study introduces biophysical “digital brain twins” constructed from resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) scans of 6,986 individuals spanning ages 18 to 100 across 16 countries.

Rather than treating brain scans as passive statistical snapshots, biophysical brain twins apply mathematical equations grounded in neurobiology to simulate how populations of excitatory and inhibitory neurons interact across 90 connected brain regions.

For each participant, the investigators tuned their computational model until its simulated fMRI output closely matched the individual’s actual resting-state brain recordings. Independent validation highlighted that model-derived regional excitability closely correlated with structural grey matter volume, confirming that the virtual simulations capture real biological architecture.

Industry observers note that “Every brain ages in a different context. Our biophysical twins help us study how the variations in our biology and the social and environmental conditions of our lives relate to brain function,” explained Ibáñez. “The importance of biophysical brain twins is that they connect what brain scans record with the underlying processes that could produce those signals. Each twin acts as a personalised virtual laboratory: researchers can adjust how its neural populations interact and examine how those changes affect the whole brain. This opens a route from observing differences to testing possible explanations, mechanisms, potential treatments and interventions.”.

In a recent development, “MRI records indirect measures of neural activity. Biophysical twins let us simulate the neural processes that might generate those signals and explore why they differ from person to person,” added Herzog.

Applying these nearly 7,000 personalized models across diverse clinical cohorts exposed clear mechanistic boundaries between normal aging and dementia:.

To overcome the historical divide between neuroimaging and real-world lived context, the team linked individual brain models with macro-level environmental indicators across 10 domains alongside personal socioeconomic histories.

Robust associations emerged in seven of the ten environmental domains, most prominently in indicators measuring democratic conditions (free choices, civic participation, political representation, and rule of law), soil and water quality, and air pollution. Complementary analyses of individual life circumstances further linked brain dynamics to healthcare access, childhood experiences, and financial stability. These relationships persisted even after controlling for age, sex, clinical diagnosis, country, and MRI scanner hardware.

By releasing their open-source code and model parameters, the authors have established a global testbed for in silico experimentation. Future studies can overlay neurotransmitter receptor maps onto these digital twins—simulating how targeted modulation of glutamate (excitatory) or GABA (inhibitory) signaling, or public health improvements in air quality and healthcare access, might shift an aging brain back toward healthy functional patterns.

What is a biophysical “digital brain twin”?

It has been revealed that A digital brain twin is a personalized computer simulation built from an individual’s fMRI scan using biological equations. By modeling how 90 connected brain regions interact, it allows researchers to estimate underlying cellular processes, such as the balance between signals that excite or inhibit neurons—and test virtual treatments safely on a computer.

How do brain dynamics differ between normal aging and dementia?

In the study of nearly 7,000 people, normal aging primarily changed how regularly or unpredictably brain activity fluctuated over time. In contrast, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal degeneration disrupted overall activity levels, variability, and the balance between excitatory and inhibitory brain signals all at once.

Can environmental and social conditions really affect how the brain functions?

According to recent reports, yes. Even after accounting for age, sex, diagnosis, and scanner differences, researchers found that environmental factors, especially democratic conditions, soil and water quality, air pollution, healthcare access, and financial circumstances, were measurably linked to underlying simulated brain dynamics.

Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype–expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.

Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological–environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics.

Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia.

In a recent development, personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure–function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes.

Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research.

These findings ground phenotypic–exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

Industry News: How to Make Better Decisions in the Age of AI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds.
  • According to recent reports, AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it.
  • Sources indicate that she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more vital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds. The power of that little “Ask anything” AI prompt box is immense, but can it help us make wiser decisions? Cheryl Strauss Einhorn, author of The Human Edge: Smarter Decisions in the Age of AI, writes:.

According to recent reports, AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it. It can illuminate pathways we might not have seen or narrow our choices in ways we do not fully recognize. As AI systems become more integrated into our lives, the challenge is no longer simply about harnessing their power but about leading them with clarity, discernment, and commitment to human agency.

Sources indicate that she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more vital. We spoke with her about why human judgment is a competitive advantage, how to engage our values when we prompt AI, and how AI can help us clarify our thinking.

Industry observers note that kia Afcari: You argue that AI makes human judgment more, not less, important. How can we make sure that the values of kindness and care are reflected when we use AI to help us make decisions?

It has been revealed that cheryl Strauss Einhorn: AI has no values. It has biases and influences by those who have designed it, and from whatever information has been fed into it. So to be sure that prosocial values are reflected when we use AI, we humans need to bring them into the work that we do together.

When working with an AI tool, we want to be asking ourselves, What is the problem that I’m solving? Why am I solving it? What is the context? And so we really need to be intentional with AI, because without asking ourselves those things first, AI doesn’t know why we’re coming to it.

Before you actually sit down with a tool, you can muster those values and those important factors related to the problem that you’re solving, and then articulate them and communicate them to the machine.

If we let the machine think for us, we can lose that sense of right and wrong, for example, because we actually care about all of those details that AI can’t possibly know about the problems that we’re solving and the people that we’re solving those problems with and for.

For example, you might ask yourself or your AI tool: Before I act, help me think through the people, relationships, and responsibilities this decision affects—not just the outcome it produces.

This type of human-centric AI interaction helped Felice, a food scientist at a pet food company, who was responsible for developing new recipes that balance nutrition, taste, and market trends. She often has to delegate tasks within her research team, ensuring that product testing, ingredient sourcing, and regulatory compliance all move forward smoothly. Using AI, she was able to analyze workloads and expertise that suggested the best person for each task, but only Felice understood the deeper dynamics at play—who works best under tight deadlines, who has a passion for innovative formulations, and who needs mentorship. When AI recommended assigning a crucial stability test to her most experienced technician, this prompt supported her thinking about a different option: giving it to the junior scientist who was eager to develop his skills in quality assurance. The AI tool’s choices made sense based on efficiency, but Felice’s decision ensured both short-term success and long-term team development.

KA: In the book, your “cheetah” metaphor celebrates slowing down. Why is a strategic pause so important when working with AI?

CSE: The cheetah metaphor relates that although this is an animal that goes zero to 60 in about three seconds, its hunting prowess actually comes from being able to decelerate up to nine miles an hour in a single stride. And the reason why that’s so important in problem solving and decision making is that’s where you build agility, flexibility, and maneuverability. Do I want to stay the course, or do I want to pivot and do something else?

This pause allows you to chunk your learning and pry open that cognitive space for upcoming information and insight. With an AI tool, it’s so crucial because there’s a difference between speed and quality.

It has been revealed that when something truly matters to us, we want to make sure that we’re solving the problem in a way that solves it holistically, that takes care of the people who are involved in the problem with us. And when we’re moving really quickly, sometimes those very important factors are hard to bring forward. So there’s a real difference between what is efficient and what is effective.

KA: Why can having more information make it harder—not easier—to make good decisions?

According to recent reports, CSE: Francis Bacon once remarked, “Knowledge is power,” but that’s not really true anymore, right? We now have all of the answers with AI to a lot of commonly asked questions and some uncommon questions.

According to recent reports, we need to make sure we’re defining the problem that we’re solving, that we are understanding and communicating the motivation and providing the context, because you don’t want all the information. Otherwise, we’re going to end up with analysis paralysis.

It has been revealed that one thing people can use is what I call the “vision of success” question. This question asks you to time travel, to jump over the decision to see that the decision has been made well. What’s happening? What are those few things that if they don’t succeed, the decision fails? It’s actually very powerful, because it allows you to clearly identify so that you can articulate those factors that you absolutely need to be able to share with AI. These become the constraints and boundaries that set the perimeter around the decision, so that it can give you research that’s targeted and focused on those things.

For example, Max deciding where to spend his next vacation. Asking AI for help directly—without turning to himself first—he got a list of destinations, airline options, and local attractions, complete with ratings, reviews, and price comparisons. On paper, that sounds ideal. But in reality, Max swiftly found himself paralyzed by the sheer amount of information. What if he picked a less-than-perfect hotel? What if he overlooked a hidden gem? AI has handed him a mountain of data, but it didn’t necessarily make the decision any easier.

However, when he used the “vision of success” question, he was able to realize and to share with his AI tool: “I want to return home feeling genuinely rested, having spent quality time with my family, without overspending or feeling like I missed the experience I was hoping for.”.

Recent findings suggest that only then does AI have a meaningful problem to solve. Instead of searching for the “best” vacation—a question with no objective answer—it can help Max find the destination most likely to produce the outcome he actually wants. AI can’t define success but it can optimize for the success you define.

It has been revealed that KA: How does the AREA method help people make wiser decisions, especially when AI is involved? CSE: AREA is more than an acronym—it’s a framework for challenging our assumptions and thinking mistakes, and actively includes the perspectives of others. It stands for Absolute, Relative, Exploration and Exploitation, and Analysis.

The first “A,” Absolute, focuses on primary, unfiltered information straight from primary sources. “R,” Relative, shifts to external viewpoints—secondary sources connected to the subject. “E,” Exploration and Exploitation, fuels creativity: Exploration broadens research through interviews and unconventional sources, while Exploitation turns inward, challenging personal biases and assumptions. The final “A,” Analysis, synthesizes everything, bringing clarity and structure to complex decisions.

When using AI, a system like AREA becomes even more crucial because AI doesn’t eliminate bias—it can reflect and sometimes amplify biases in its training data, design, and the way we use it. Good decisions require a process that helps us recognize and challenge both AI’s biases and our own.

For AI, so much of the information, for example, is from Reddit. Information can be incomplete or outdated, and you also know that you’re interacting with a liar. It’s a machine that just gives you answers that are wrong sometimes.

According to recent reports, so you need to be able to have a quality due diligence process to not only be able to use the tool effectively, but to be able to evaluate its outcome. Too often, people look at an answer with AI and think that it’s a transaction, and they can just take it. AREA is going to help you make sure that it’s a conversation. So you have an evidence-based perspective that has looked at a variety of stakeholder viewpoints, and made sure that you have pried open that cognitive space to challenge the natural, well-worn mental pathways that we all lean on every day.

KA: How can we use AI in ways that strengthen—rather than undermine—our values and agency?

It has been revealed that CSE: It’s a great question. I think the new competitive advantage is going to be self-awareness.

This is the first tool that actually asks for some of our cognitive load; it wants us to offload some of our decisions to it. And this is a machine fundamentally about decision making, because we ask it for something and it gives us an answer. But there’s a very interesting invitation here, which is to each of us to get to know ourselves better.

Industry observers note that we each have a special sauce, which is the way that we make our decisions, and we make thousands of them every single day. But most of us have not sat down and noted to themselves, What does that process actually look like? Can I actually name those pieces and put language to it?

There is this invitation to get to know our thinking so that we can translate it better, and not only for the tool. How helpful would it be in conversation with our colleagues to be able to say clearly, This is how I’m actually going through the steps, this is how I’m thinking about it, these are the variables that I’m prioritizing, and here’s what I think is the most diagnostic.

Sources indicate that you can think about your thinking skills as muscles. If we turn over our cognitive load, we will also weaken it. But if we actually take this invitation to understand our self-awareness and our metacognition, we can make sure that we strengthen those tools.

AI is a tool that has so many implications for our environment and for our world, in addition to the fact that it has implications for our actual thinking skills.

So I would say that the invitation is to turn to yourself first. Ask yourself why you’re using the tool, and whether or not you should be turning to yourself instead. And either way, bring your own thinking forward before sitting down, so that you can feel far more comfortable that you can problem-solve both with it and beyond it.

The Brain Creates Body Ownership Before Touch Occurs

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that researchers have mapped the exact millisecond-by-millisecond sequence of brain activity that creates the feeling that a hand belongs to our own body.
  • In a recent development, we effortlessly take for granted that our hands, arms, and limbs belong to us.
  • While prior neuroimaging studies identified the general brain regions involved in self-perception, the exact temporal choreography, when each region activates and how signals cascade across the cortex, has remained elusive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that researchers have mapped the exact millisecond-by-millisecond sequence of brain activity that creates the feeling that a hand belongs to our own body. The magnetoencephalography (MEG) study reveals three distinct neural phases, beginning even before physical touch occurs, and explains why right-hemisphere strokes frequently cause patients to disown their left arm.

In a recent development, we effortlessly take for granted that our hands, arms, and limbs belong to us. Yet this seamless sense of body ownership is an active perceptual construction, one that requires the brain to continuously merge visual, tactile, and spatial signals in real time, and one that can shatter dramatically following neurological injury.

While prior neuroimaging studies identified the general brain regions involved in self-perception, the exact temporal choreography, when each region activates and how signals cascade across the cortex, has remained elusive.

Now, in a study published in Nature Communications, neuroscientists at Karolinska Institutet led by Professor Henrik Ehrsson (Department of Neuroscience) and co-author Professor Daniel Lundqvist (Department of Clinical Neuroscience) have charted the birth of body ownership millisecond by millisecond.

To capture how the brain constructs the feeling that a limb is its own, the team recruited 45 healthy volunteers for a precision robotic version of the classic rubber hand illusion.

Participants watched a lifelike artificial hand resting in front of them while their real left hand remained hidden behind a screen. Two robotic arms delivered brief, synchronized touches to both the visible rubber hand and the concealed real hand, while high-speed magnetoencephalography (MEG) recorded whole-brain magnetic fields. By comparing synchronized touches (which trigger the illusion that the rubber hand is part of one’s body) against asynchronous touches and real-hand control conditions, the researchers isolated the neural signature of body ownership across the 28 participants who vividly experienced the illusion.

Reconstructing brain activity every four milliseconds produced a real-time movie of self-perception unfolding across three distinct phases:.

“We know quite a lot about which areas of the brain are involved in the sense that the body is our own, but considerably less about when different areas become active and how they interact. We have now been able to track how activity patterns in the brain develop over time,” explained Ehrsson.

“The fact that the activity began even before the hand was touched shows that the brain’s expectations of what we are going to feel are closely linked to the conscious experience of the body as our own,” added Lundqvist. “This study shows when, in what order, and how different brain regions help combine information from different senses into a unified experience of our own body.”.

According to recent reports, notably, during the first two phases of the sequence, neural activity was confined almost entirely to the right hemisphere. This lateralized timing aligns strikingly with clinical neurology: following a stroke, patients who experience somatoparaphrenia, the disturbing condition in which a limb no longer feels like part of one’s own body, almost always disown their left arm after damage to the right hemisphere.

“When stroke patients lose the sense that an arm belongs to them, it is usually the left arm that is affected, following damage to the right hemisphere of the brain,” Ehrsson noted. “In future studies, we want to compare patterns of brain activity associated with the right and left hands to better understand the different roles of the brain’s hemispheres. We also want to collaborate with stroke researchers to investigate this phenomenon in patients.”.

How does the brain create the feeling that your hand belongs to your body?

Industry observers note that karolinska Institutet researchers found that body ownership arises through a precise three-stage sequence of brain activity. It starts with predictive expectation before a hand is even touched, sweeps rapidly across the right frontal, parietal, and cerebellar regions, and finally engages the left hemisphere to unify sensory information.

Why did brain activity start before the hand was physically touched?

It has been revealed that seeing an object approach the hand triggers predictive brain activity based on what we expect to feel. This pre-touch expectation primes the brain to merge sight and touch into the conscious experience that the limb is our own.

How does this study help explain disturbed body perception after a stroke?

Because the first two critical stages of body ownership occur almost exclusively in the brain’s right hemisphere, damage to that side from a stroke disrupts the early multisensory integration needed to recognize the left arm, explaining why stroke patients frequently lose the sense that their left arm belongs to them.

Sources indicate that funding: The study was funded by the Swedish Research Council, the Göran Gustafsson Foundation, the Torsten Söderberg Foundation and the Swedish Brain Foundation. NatMEG receives support from the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation. The researchers declare no conflicts of interest.

Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception.

We experience our limbs as our own, but how does the brain generate this fundamental sense of body ownership?

Previous studies have relied mainly on fMRI or lesion mapping, providing a static view of the neural mechanisms underlying body ownership.

Using magnetoencephalography, robotically controlled visuotactile stimulation, and multivariate analysis across the rubber hand illusion, a real hand condition, and multiple control conditions, we identified source vector dissimilarity patterns reflecting ownership of the left arm.

Three phases of ownership-specific activity patterns emerged: (i) anticipatory patterns in medial frontal cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and right posterior cerebellum before tactile stimulation; (ii) multisensory integration patterns in right dorsal and ventral premotor cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and anterior cerebellum at 116–156 ms poststimulus; and (iii) later bilateral insular and left hemisphere patterns at 184–232 ms.

These findings provide a whole-brain, time-resolved map of activity patterns underlying body ownership, revealing its dynamic neural construction.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that for the roughly one in five Americans living with a mental health condition, frontline psychiatric medications have changed remarkably little since the 1950s.
  • Against this backdrop, psychedelic compounds, including classic serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin and dissociative agents like ketamine, have sparked intense clinical excitement for their ability to produce rapid, durable improvements in mood, addiction, and post-traumatic stress disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New neuroscience research reveals that both psilocybin and ketamine improve decision accuracy by helping the brain rely less on rigid, repetitive habits and more on real-time sensory cues. The study highlights that rather than scrambling neural signaling, these compounds gently sculpt ongoing brain activity, trading a slight reduction in reaction speed for sharper, more flexible choices.

Industry observers note that for the roughly one in five Americans living with a mental health condition, frontline psychiatric medications have changed remarkably little since the 1950s. Conventional antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) often require weeks to take effect, demand chronic daily use, and fail to provide adequate relief for roughly 30% of patients with treatment-resistant depression.

Against this backdrop, psychedelic compounds, including classic serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin and dissociative agents like ketamine, have sparked intense clinical excitement for their ability to produce rapid, durable improvements in mood, addiction, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Yet precisely how these drugs alter neural circuits to break entrenched patterns of negative thinking has remained poorly understood.

In a recent development, now, in a study published in Science Advances, neuroscientists at Boston University led by assistant professor Dr. Benjamin Scott and associate professor Dr. Steve Ramirez have uncovered a shared pro-cognitive mechanism linking psilocybin and ketamine: both drugs weaken the brain’s reliance on automatic habits and heighten sensitivity to immediate sensory cues.

To test how psychedelics influence moment-to-moment decision-making, Scott, Ramirez, and colleagues trained mice on a perceptual task requiring the animals to use brief pulses of light to identify which of two ports contained a reward.

Untreated mice performed the task moderately well, but frequently fell into habitual traps—repeatedly returning to a previously rewarded location even when the light cues clearly signaled a change. Following administration of either psilocybin or ketamine, however, mice made significantly fewer errors. Rather than falling back on repetitive choice biases, treated animals anchored their decisions much more closely to real-time sensory information.

“These findings reveal how psychedelics reduce the reliance on habits and repetitive choices, which may explain part of their therapeutic effect,” explained Scott, a faculty member in Boston University’s Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences.

Although psilocybin acts primarily on serotonin receptors (such as 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A) while ketamine blocks glutamate NMDA receptors, their behavioral effects converged on sharper, less biased decision-making.

To observe what changed inside the brain, the researchers combined brain-wide genetic activity mapping with targeted neural recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a prefrontal region essential for evaluating rewards, making decisions, and updating beliefs when rules change.

Recent findings suggest that remarkably, psilocybin did not erase or scramble existing task representations. Instead, core OFC activity patterns tracking sensory cues and choices remained largely intact, accompanied by widespread yet subtle adjustments across interconnected brain regions. According to the authors, this gentle sculpting of ongoing neural activity aligns closely with clinical observations that a person’s mindset and environment (“set and setting”) strongly shape the psychedelic experience.

The team also identified an key behavioral nuance: while mice made more accurate choices after receiving psilocybin or ketamine, they took longer to deliberate, revealing a classic speed-accuracy tradeoff. While slower deliberation can benefit reflective cognitive therapy, it underscores why activities demanding split-second reaction times, such as driving, are unsafe under the influence of these compounds.

Looking ahead, Scott and Ramirez initiative to pinpoint the exact neural pathways responsible for breaking rigid habits, with the ultimate goal of developing targeted, next-generation therapies that unlock cognitive flexibility without hallucinogenic side effects.

How do psilocybin and ketamine improve decision-making in this study?

Boston University researchers found that both drugs help the brain pay closer attention to immediate sensory cues (like flashes of light) while reducing the tendency to fall back on repetitive habits, leading to significantly more accurate choices.

Do psychedelics scramble normal brain activity during a task?

No. Recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex showed that the brain’s core patterns for tracking cues and making decisions remained largely preserved. Instead of causing chaos, psilocybin induced widespread yet subtle shifts that gently sculpted how the brain updated its beliefs.

Were there any downsides to the improved decision accuracy?

Yes. Researchers observed a speed-accuracy tradeoff: while treated animals made fewer mistakes, they took longer to make their decisions, suggesting these compounds slow down reaction times even as they promote more deliberative thinking.

Psychedelics Shift Decision Strategies and Reconfigure Orbitofrontal Dynamics.

Psychedelics such as psilocybin and ketamine are attracting renewed attention as rapid-acting therapeutics, yet how they reshape cognitive computations remains poorly understood.

According to recent reports, to address this, we trained mice on a free-response perceptual decision-making task that disentangles bias-driven from sensory-guided strategies. Acute administration of psilocybin or ketamine slowed decision times while improving accuracy. Behavioral modeling combining drift diffusion and GLM-HMM approaches revealed that these effects were driven by increased decision thresholds and a shift toward sensory-engaged states.

Industry observers note that whole-brain c-Fos mapping identified modulation of distributed task-related networks, including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Calcium imaging revealed that OFC population dynamics were reorganized under psychedelic conditions, with preserved task selectivity but altered temporal structure and shifted population correlations.

Together, these findings indicate that psychedelics shift decision-making toward greater reliance on sensory evidence while reshaping cortical population dynamics, providing a system-level account of their effects on perceptual decisions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.

Dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds. In the Bistro night scene, standard three.js under WebGL leaves the cobblestones cool and flat, with a blown-out white hotspot around the round shop sign. Even with WebGPU and SSGI turned on, the lamp glare stays harsh and the pavement loses multi-bounce warmth. Slide the divider across to ThreeRT, and warm golden light spills from the shop window across the facade while overhead string lights tint the street in their own colors.

The Zero-Day sci-fi corridor reveals an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline. On the three.js side, ceiling pipes and glossy floors pick up heavy speckle noise, and unlit industrial housings sink into dark blue shadows. ThreeRT keeps those white and grey panels legible through soft indirect bounce light from tiny amber emitters. It doesn't rely on light probes or baked maps, so moving the camera at 60 fps never breaks the reflections of off-screen geometry.

Recent findings suggest that that matters for the future of ray tracing in the browser. Today, ThreeRT runs its Rust and wgpu path tracer inside a native client while exposing a familiar three.js-style TypeScript API. The same scene code still runs as plain three.js in any browser or WebView, which gives developers one codebase across both worlds. As WebGPU hardware ray tracing matures on the web, that gap is closing fast.

It has been revealed that you can see the range in the project gallery, from the OpenStrikeRT foundry hall where a furnace lights the surrounding concrete, to smaller studies like Jeweller's Window, Daylight Home, and Boutique Showroom. Each surface reacts to real emitters instead of faked ambient fill. See the full project on ThreeRTâs website.

#91881. Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?
