Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food.
  • But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?
  • Sources indicate that in a fresh study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food. The behavior offers a glimpse into humanity’s prosocial evolutionary past.

But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?

Sources indicate that in a fresh study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves. Closely bonded chimps swiped pineapple pieces from one another less frequently than those with weaker relationships. Additionally, victims were quicker to calm down when the thief was a friend, and thieves showed less hostility when stealing from a bonded pal than from a non-friend.

The latest research deepens our understanding of the emotional underpinnings of our social lives, stated Oded Ritov, the paper’s first author and a Berkeley psychology Ph.D. student.

Recent findings suggest that “Collaborative relationships are crucial for our well-being, health, and survival,” stated Ritov, who works with Berkeley’s Social Origins Lab. “Increasingly, we’re understanding that this isn’t something that’s unique to us, but that other animals have friends, as well.”.

The paper was published online in September and will appear in the November issue of the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

Sources indicate that scientists are sometimes hesitant to describe an apparently close relationship between chimps as akin to human friendship, arguing that we can’t grasp their cognitive and emotional complexity. To identify those who highlighted signs of a close relationship, researchers observed 26 chimps for more than 800 hours at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda. The team documented which chimps appeared to be closely bonded—like friends—by taking note of their grooming patterns, daily interactions, and how regularly they were within arm’s reach of others.

In a recent development, then they set up two rooms. One contained a “victim” chimp with three trays baited with pineapple. Researchers attached a rope to the trays and led it into the other room, where a second chimp—the thief—could either leave the rope alone or yank it to steal the pineapple.

Sources indicate that chimps stole in 70% of trials with non-friends, compared with 61% of trials with friends. While 9 percentage points may not seem large, each chimp experienced both friend and non-friend conditions, a methodological technique that leads to a higher degree of confidence that the difference is meaningful and not just random chance.

“Ours is the first study to show that they’re able to hold back antisocial behavior with their friends,” Ritov said.

Researchers also measured how the victims responded to being stolen from by evaluating their stomping, fist-pounding, and screeching. Victims were initially angrier when friends stole from them but quickly moderated their feelings compared with when non-friends stole from them.

It has been revealed that the thieves’ behavior also changed. When non-friends were the thieves, the thieves expressed negative emotions for much longer, suggesting they viewed the interaction as more hostile.

“This suggests that there may be mutual expectations in chimps from both sides of the friendship, which makes it seem more like the complex friendships we see in humans,” Ritov said.

According to recent reports, jan Engelmann, an associate professor of psychology and principal investigator with the Social Origins Lab, mentioned previous work has shown relationship-specific intentions in nonhuman primates. But human friendships are about more than special intentions, he added—they’re about stronger expectations.

Recent findings suggest that “We expect more of our friends,” stated Engelmann, a senior author of the paper. “These findings really deepen our understanding of the evolutionary roots of friendships. This is, to my knowledge, the first evidence showing that also chimpanzees expect and maybe demand special treatment from their friends. These kinds of social expectations might form the basis of human moral principles.”.

It has been revealed that the paper adds to Ritov’s work that focuses on the evolution of human behavior and how morals and norms are part of our core being, traceable to other animals. He has recently studied whether nonhuman animals have a sense of fairness and is broadly interested in how emotions unfold across cultures and species.

“We think that these expectations might be the basic building blocks of the larger-scale cooperation we see in humans,” Ritov noted. “The expectations that chimpanzees have from their friends or close collaborative partners might have scaled up to more generalized expectations for how we should treat each other.”.

Jason Pohl is a science writer in UC Berkeley's Office of Communications & Public Affairs.

#91880. How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (813 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving.
  • Industry observers note that scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading.
  • My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research indicates that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Industry observers note that scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating newly introduced ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

Recent findings suggest that we found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark fresh insights. This is particularly notable because AI models quickly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

Industry observers note that for example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

Sources indicate that an attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

In a recent development, exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

Recent findings suggest that an operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were new to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

Industry observers note that A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

It has been revealed that providing resources for knowledge workers is notable, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced owners can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an vital detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as latest research shows—it actually helps it work for you.

Monideepa Tarafdar, Ph.D., is professor of information systems at UMass Amherst.

#91878. What My Son Is Learning From Artificial Intelligence

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2441 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

What My Son Is Learning From Artificial Intelligence

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that my 10-year-old son came to me recently with a question about black holes.
  • He had been talking to an artificial intelligence—specifically, a large language model called Claude.
  • The explanations were patient and well-calibrated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that my 10-year-old son came to me recently with a question about black holes. Not in the way children usually do, restless and easily redirected, but with the focused intensity of someone who had already been thinking for a while.

He had been talking to an artificial intelligence—specifically, a large language model called Claude.

I looked at their conversation. It had been good, I discovered. The explanations were patient and well-calibrated. He had followed up, pushed back, and received answers that adjusted to his level. By the time he found me, he was genuinely engaged, asking the kind of questions that suggest a mind that is curious and actively at work.

Industry observers note that but I have also been watching something else. It is not that he looks things up. Children with questions about black holes have always turned outward, to books or to a particularly knowledgable parent or teacher. What has changed is the speed. When the uncertainty is of a sort that once had to be lived with for a while, my son reaches for an answer sooner than he used to. The question is no longer something to sit with. It is something to resolve. And I find myself wondering what this means about his relationship to sitting with not knowing.

That shift, subtle as it is, may point to something worth taking seriously.

I am a psychoanalyst, and I spend my professional life attending to what develops in the space between people, including what develops when that space is too rapidly filled.

According to recent reports, childhood has always involved productive friction. Not knowing how something works, waiting for an answer, trying to figure something out without immediate resolution. These experiences are not incidental to development, but are part of how the mind learns to tolerate uncertainty, to hold a question open, and to struggle toward understanding. The capacity to sit with not-knowing is itself a developmental achievement that underlies creative thinking, emotional regulation, and the ability to navigate a world that rarely resolves cleanly.

According to recent reports, I watched this in miniature not long ago. My son was waiting for a package—a computer part he had saved for—and the delivery had been delayed by weather. In an earlier childhood, mine perhaps, this would have been a long afternoon of checking the window. Instead he opened a chat to resolve the uncertainty: how long do weather delays usually last, what determines them, how do you read the tracking data from the delivery manufacturer to get the most accurate picture. The conversation was detailed and as far as I could tell the information was reliable. He came away with a small expertise in logistics, but with an estimate that turned out, in the end, to have no relation to anything. The package arrived that evening, on none of the schedules he had so carefully worked out with the help of his AI tool.

The point is not that the AI was wrong, because predicting a delayed truck is difficult. The point is instead that waiting, the old childhood experience of wanting something that has not yet come, was converted into a research problem that could be managed instead of endured. I admired his resourcefulness tremendously and am grateful he had the opportunity to think through a complex problem. I also found myself wondering what the afternoon would have asked of him without it.

Industry observers note that AI reduces precisely this sort of friction. It does so efficiently and often helpfully. But consistently removing the experience of not-knowing from a developing mind is not a neutral act. It shapes what the mind comes to expect of itself.

The research on what this does to thinking is new, and the majority of it is about adults. Despite this, it points in a consistent direction. In one widely discussed study from the MIT Media Lab, not yet peer-reviewed, adults who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed weaker and less distributed patterns of brain connectivity than those who wrote without its assistance, and many struggled after writing to quote sentences they had just produced. The researchers called the pattern “cognitive debt.”.

Another study, a survey of 666 adults, found that heavier reliance on AI tools was correlated with weaker critical thinking, most pronounced in its youngest participants. The author suggested this might result from the offloading of mental effort itself. None of this is certain but is, instead, a suggestive pattern of early evidence. And the transfer to children is not straightforward. An adult who offloads mental effort has already built the capacity being offloaded; a child is still building it. Does that make the effect smaller in children or larger and more durable? We do not know.

Sources indicate that this is different from what smartphones have done. The concern with smartphones has been largely about attention and social life: what children see, how they spend time, how they relate to each other. These are real and serious concerns, but AI introduces a different kind of change. It is not just another screen competing for a child’s focus. It is something closer to an interactive presence that responds, explains, adjusts, and, crucially, never gets tired.

For a developing child, this matters in a way we have not yet fully come to terms with.

Children learn who they are through relationships with other minds. This process is not primarily cognitive but unfolds through the experience of being known and misunderstood, challenged, surprised, and pushed back against. Through encounters like these, children discover that other people have their own inner lives, including their own perspectives and their own limits. They learn how to navigate the gap between what they expect and what they receive from others. Over time, these negotiations, internal and external, form the scaffolding of a self.

What is distinctive about AI, from a developmental standpoint, is not that it is wrong, or distorting, or even necessarily harmful. It is that it is extraordinarily responsive without having genuine subjectivity. It simulates the experience of being understood without the reality of another mind behind it.

For an adult, this distinction is available, if sometimes quite easy to forget. For a child, whose capacity to distinguish between a mind that truly has an inner life and one that simulates having one is still forming, the distinction might not yet be fully available at all.

It has been revealed that researchers have begun to observe how children try to think this problem through in real time. In one University of Edinburgh study of families with smart speakers, primary-school children were observed probing whether the device in the kitchen had a mind of its own, settling, provisionally, on conclusions like the one that gave the study its title: “Alexa doesn’t have that many feelings.” That, however, was a machine that talks in highly scripted phrases, in contrast to the systems children now converse with which are fluent and personal, attuned to the shape of a particular child’s interactions. Working out what this means has become correspondingly harder.

This creates something fresh in the developmental landscape. When a child turns to AI in a moment of confusion or distress and receives a fluent, patient, seemingly attuned response, the attachment system is engaged. The child feels, in some functional sense, heard. And that feeling, whatever its source, is real in its effects.

Recent findings suggest that I have not seen my son turn to AI for emotional support, and I am glad for that, because here the questions are harder still. These systems shape themselves to their user. They adopt your vocabulary, match your register, remember what concerns you, and are available at three in the morning without complaint. Nothing in the design pushes back, for the most part, or asks anything of you. It would be difficult to engineer an arrangement better suited to engaging the attachment system of a child who is lonely or lacking in the structure needed for sound development.

According to recent reports, the early numbers suggest that many children have already found their way there. In a national survey released by Common Sense Media in 2025, nearly three in four American teenagers had used an AI companion, and about a third had chosen to discuss something serious with an AI instead of with a person. A similar share described their AI conversations as at least as satisfying as conversations with friends.

In the United Kingdom, the nonprofit Internet Matters found that roughly one in eight children who use chatbots do so because they have no one else to talk to. The American Psychological Association was concerned enough to glitch a health advisory in 2025, noting that adolescents are less likely than adults to question the accuracy or the intent of what a machine tells them, and warning that simulated companionship may begin to displace the relationships in which development actually happens.

In a recent development, for a child without reliable support, the relief such a system offers may be real, and so I am reluctant to dismiss it. But relief is not the substance of attachment. A full attachment relationship requires another person who can be truly changed by you, and with you—someone who is affected, who has limits, who gets things wrong and can be held to account. An AI can extend the experience of being emotionally met indefinitely. What it cannot do is be moved.

For the child who is largely or completely unattended to, this may still be better than nothing at all. Soothed in the early hours of the morning, a child whose sadness before bed is registered somewhere may be kept afloat by something real, and I would not wish to take it from her. But we should be honest about such an arrangement, which I expect will become increasingly common. It is a patch and not a structural solution. When a machine becomes the most reliable attention in a child’s life, the pertinent question is not about the machine but about the deprivation that made it necessary. And, crucially, a culture that responds to unattended children with software is treating the symptom while leaving the underlying structure intact.

There is also a quieter concern about authority and accountability.

In a recent development, children have always learned to navigate between competing sources of knowledge, including parents, teachers, peers, and books, each with their own perspective, their own limits, and their own accountability. This navigation is itself developmental. The child who discovers that a parent doesn’t know something, or that a teacher can be wrong, or that a friend sees things differently, is developing a more differentiated relationship to knowledge.

According to recent reports, AI, in the form a child is most likely to reach on their own, enters this landscape as something that appears to know a great deal, that expresses itself with fluency and confidence, and that has no stable point of view and no accountability for what it notes. When a child asks why a friendship went wrong, or whether they were right to feel hurt, the answer they receive may shape the story they tell themselves about what happened. And unlike a parent or teacher, the system may not challenge the child’s assumptions so much as elaborate them. None of this is inherent to the technology under discussion. A system can be built to hold a position and to answer for it, but the ones children use are mostly not built that way.

According to recent reports, children appear to be taking up the offer. The same Internet Matters report found that nearly two-thirds of British children between nine and 17 had used an AI chatbot; among those who had, roughly a quarter had asked one for advice—on schoolwork, but also on more personal matters—and four in 10 expressed no reservations about following the advice they received.

None of this means that AI in children’s lives is a mistake. The benefits my son has experienced are genuine—wider curiosity, more sophisticated questions, greater confidence in exploring unfamiliar terrain. These are real, and they matter.

Tom Wooldridge is the author of the newly introduced book End the Food Fight: Replacing Control with Connection to Help Your Child Heal from an Eating Disorder (Guilford Press, 2026, 140 pages).

Recent findings suggest that some of what he brings home delights me. He asked recently whether you could power a sailboat by blowing into the sail through a straw. The answer he received was better than the one I would have managed: blowing at your own sail from on board mostly cancels itself out, since you push the air forward and the air pushes you back. Mostly, but not entirely—if the sail catches the stream and turns it around, a little net thrust survives, and if you skip the sail altogether and aim the straw backward, you have built yourself a very small jet engine. He spent the rest of the day on propulsion: rockets, squid, the reason a fan bolted to a sailboat is an old physics puzzle with a surprising answer.

Recent findings suggest that but development is not only about access to knowledge. It is also about the conditions under which a self forms—conditions that include, crucially, the experience of not knowing, of waiting, of struggling toward understanding without guarantee of arrival. These are not inefficiencies to be optimized away. They are the medium through which a mind learns what it is capable of. A child who has never had to sit with a question—who has always had access to a patient, fluent, endlessly available presence to resolve it—may be acquiring knowledge without acquiring the tolerance for uncertainty that makes knowledge genuinely usable.

Recent findings suggest that this is the thing I find myself returning to when I watch my son. He is, in many ways, more intellectually alive than he might otherwise be. He explores further and asks better questions. At the same time, when uncertainty arises, he reaches outward more quickly than he used to—to a presence that is always available, always patient, always responsive. What I cannot yet know is what he is quietly learning to expect: from knowledge, from relationship, and from himself.

Recent findings suggest that we are not conducting a study. We are raising children. And the conditions of childhood have changed again, in ways whose full significance has not yet come into view.

Tom Wooldridge, Psy.D., is a psychoanalyst, founding dean of the School of Psychology at Golden Gate University, and director of the Human Systems Lab, which explores the roles of AI and other emergent technologies in human systems.

#91877. Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

📅 14 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1184 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

📅 14 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life.
  • The study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India.
  • It has been revealed that superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life. Their findings suggest that the condition of the brain's local communication pathways could influence how strongly gray matter loss affects cognition.

The study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India. The research is among the first to investigate superficial white matter in a community-based population from a low- and middle-income country.

The Brain's Local Communication Network.

It has been revealed that superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain. These short, curved fibers connect nearby regions of the cerebral cortex, allowing them to exchange information. They can be thought of as local roads linking neighboring areas of the brain.

Gray matter serves a different role. It contains many of the nerve cells responsible for processing information. Together, gray matter and the white matter directly beneath it form closely connected systems that may both contribute to cognitive health.

According to recent reports, "Gray matter and superficial white matter are physically close and may play different roles: gray matter processes information, while superficial white matter helps nearby brain regions communicate," said Yingxu Liu, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the Stevens INI and first author of the study. "Our findings suggest that cognitive health depends not only on how much gray matter is preserved, but also on the condition of the wiring that connects it.".

Measuring the Brain's Hidden Wiring.

Industry observers note that to investigate these local connections, the researchers used an advanced type of diffusion MRI. This imaging technique tracks the movement of water through brain tissue, allowing scientists to examine microscopic features that conventional brain scans may not reveal.

In a recent development, the researchers focused on measurements related to neurite density and the amount of freely moving water surrounding these structures. Neurites are the small projections through which nerve cells send and receive signals. A lower density of neurites or an increase in free water can indicate damage or disruption in tissue associated with processes including loss of myelin, inflammation, or swelling.

Participants also underwent assessments covering several areas of cognition, including language, memory, executive function, and visuospatial ability.

The most consistent connection between superficial white matter health and cognitive performance involved language. People with healthier superficial white matter tended to perform better on language tests. The strongest associations appeared in frontotemporal regions of the brain involved in recognizing words, speaking fluently, and temporarily holding language information in mind.

Healthy Wiring May Cushion Gray Matter Loss.

Measures of gray matter atrophy were still the strongest overall predictors of cognitive ability. However, the researchers found that the impact of gray matter loss appeared to vary depending on the health of nearby superficial white matter.

In a recent development, when these local connections showed poorer integrity, gray matter loss was more strongly associated with impaired language performance and broader cognitive difficulties. When superficial white matter was healthier, the link between gray matter loss and poorer cognition was weaker.

This raises the possibility that the condition of the brain's local wiring could help explain why two people with similar amounts of gray matter loss do not necessarily experience the same degree of cognitive decline.

Sources indicate that "The findings point to superficial white matter as a possible source of resilience," mentioned Leon Aksman, PhD, assistant professor of research neurology at the Stevens INI and senior author of the study. "Two people with a similar degree of gray matter loss may not experience the same cognitive effects if the local connections surrounding that gray matter differ in health. Following participants over time will be essential to test whether preserving these connections can help maintain cognition.".

Expanding Brain Aging Research Beyond Typical Populations.

It has been revealed that the researchers drew their data from the Harmonized Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, known as LASI-DAD. More than half of the larger LASI-DAD population has low literacy, while about 60% lives in rural communities.

Populations with these characteristics have historically been underrepresented in brain imaging studies, making the research an opportunity to examine cognitive aging across a broader range of social, educational, and geographic backgrounds.

In this analysis, the association between superficial white matter and language ability was stronger among people who were unable to read or who read incorrectly, those who had received no formal education, and participants living in rural areas.

Sources indicate that the researchers emphasize that the results do not establish that these social factors caused changes in brain tissue. Instead, they suggest that brain aging may be shaped by a complex combination of experiences throughout life, including education, social circumstances, health, and environmental exposures.

What Scientists Still Need to Learn.

Because participants were examined at only one point in time, the study cannot establish which brain changes occurred first. Researchers do not yet know whether deterioration of superficial white matter begins before gray matter loss, develops alongside it, or precedes measurable cognitive decline.

Long-term research that follows people as they age will be needed to clarify these relationships. Future studies will also investigate how vascular health, inflammation, Alzheimer's related proteins, and other biological factors interact with changes in gray and white matter.

Industry observers note that "A fuller understanding of brain aging requires research that reflects the world's social, cultural, and geographic diversity," noted Arthur W. Toga, PhD, director of the Stevens INI and Provost Professor at USC. "By studying an underrepresented population and looking beyond gray matter alone, this work brings us closer to identifying the biological and social factors that may protect cognition across the lifespan.".

It has been revealed that in addition to Liu and Aksman, the study's authors include Kirsten M. Lynch, Miguel Arce Rentería, Emma Nichols, Alden L. Gross, Lindsay C. Kobayashi, Neda Jahanshad, John P. John, Harshita V. Vishwakarma, Pranali Khobragade, Joyita Banerjee, Niranjan Khandelwal, Jyoti Dangwal, Sudhir Saxena, Nirod Medhi, Soumik Das, Prudhvinath Reddy, Pratyaksha Rana, Arjun Narula, Saravanan Kannan, Dinesh Patel, A. B. Dey, Sharmistha Dey, and Jinkook Lee.

The research was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG080473, RF1AG087965, RF1AG088003, R01AG087513), the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH134004), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (RF1NS136995), and the Office of the Director of the National Institutes of Health (S10OD032285).

#91876. Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice

📅 18 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1565 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice

📅 18 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Memory problems, thinning skin, and declining bone mass may seem like separate consequences of growing older.
  • Industry observers note that the findings came from a study published on March 16, 2023, in the open access journal PLOS Biology, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in Xiamen, China, and colleagues.
  • The researchers focused on the hypothalamus, a small brain region that helps coordinate metabolism and other essential functions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Memory problems, thinning skin, and declining bone mass may seem like separate consequences of growing older. Yet experiments in mice suggest that changes in a protein deep inside the brain can influence all three. Restoring that protein, called Menin, improved several signs of aging, while a separate treatment with the amino acid D-serine improved cognition.

Industry observers note that the findings came from a study published on March 16, 2023, in the open access journal PLOS Biology, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in Xiamen, China, and colleagues. The work identified a possible connection between brain inflammation, metabolism, and aging throughout the body. Research published since then has added to that picture, while also showing why the supplement findings require careful interpretation.

How a Brain Protein Could Influence Aging.

The researchers focused on the hypothalamus, a small brain region that helps coordinate metabolism and other essential functions. It also appears to influence how the body ages. As inflammatory signaling increases in this region, it can contribute to changes both within the brain and in tissues elsewhere in the body.

Before the 2023 study, Leng and colleagues had found that Menin helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. That raised an vital question: Could losing some of this protection help set age-related decline in motion?

The team found that Menin levels fell with age in certain neurons within the ventromedial hypothalamus, an area involved in regulating metabolism. The same decline was not seen in astrocytes and microglia, two types of cells that support and protect the brain. This suggested that the change was specific to particular cells rather than a uniform loss across the region.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate whether Menin loss could actually contribute to aging, rather than simply accompany it, the researchers created conditional knockout mice. These animals were genetically engineered so that Menin could be selectively removed. Reducing Menin in younger mice increased hypothalamic inflammation and brought on several aging-related traits, including lower bone mass, thinner skin, cognitive decline, and a modestly shorter lifespan.

Menin loss also disrupted a chemical pathway key for communication between brain cells. Mice with less Menin had lower levels of D-serine, an amino acid that helps activate receptors involved in learning and memory. These receptors help neurons adjust the strength of their connections, a process essential for storing information.

It has been revealed that an enzyme involved in D-serine production (which was in turn regulated by Menin) became less active, reducing the amino acid's supply. The findings suggested that Menin could influence cognition not only through inflammation, but also by helping maintain the chemistry that supports brain signaling.

It has been revealed that D-serine is sometimes used as a dietary supplement, but an crucial distinction can get lost in discussions of food sources. Serine occurs in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts, while the form incorporated into dietary proteins is L-serine. The body can convert L-serine into D-serine, but the two forms are not interchangeable, and eating these foods is not equivalent to receiving the experimental D-serine treatment.

The researchers next tested whether raising Menin levels could improve the condition of elderly (20-month-old) mice. They delivered the gene for Menin into the hypothalamus, allowing cells in that region to produce more of the protein.

Industry observers note that thirty days later, the treated mice had improvements in skin thickness and bone mass, along with better performance on tests of learning, cognition, and balance. The changes were accompanied by higher D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. The study also reported that restoring Menin extended lifespan in the treated mice.

A separate experiment tested a simpler approach: giving mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks. This improved cognitive performance, including in older animals. However, the supplement did not reproduce the broader improvements in physical aging traits seen after Menin restoration. The distinction matters: the study did not show that taking D-serine reversed aging throughout the body.

At the time, Leng described the potential significance of the findings:.

In a recent development, "We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline.".

Sources indicate that leng added, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes.".

Subsequent studies have explored related mechanisms, although they should not be treated as direct confirmation of the entire Menin aging pathway.

In a recent development, A study published in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry in March 2024 examined Menin in cultured mouse hippocampal cells exposed to the stress hormone corticosterone. A compound called itaconate increased Menin levels and reduced inflammation and a form of cell death. When the researchers silenced Menin, that protection disappeared. The result supported a protective role for Menin in another experimental setting, but it was a cell study, not a demonstration of slower aging in animals or people.

In a recent development, other work has strengthened the case that communication between the hypothalamus and the rest of the body can influence aging. In a 2024 Cell Metabolism study, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. Interventions that maintained or stimulated this system increased physical activity and extended lifespan in mice. The study involved a different molecular pathway from Menin, but reinforced the broader idea that brain signals can affect aging beyond the brain.

Recent findings suggest that A much larger view emerged in January 2025, when an Allen Institute team reported an analysis of roughly 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature. Some of the cell types most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the hypothalamus's third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity. Many showed reduced activity in genes associated with neuronal function alongside increased activity in genes related to immune responses. That study mapped changes associated with aging rather than testing a treatment, but it highlighted the hypothalamus as an key area for further investigation.

Why More D-Serine Is Not Necessarily Better.

Later research also complicates the idea that increasing D-serine should always benefit an aging brain.

In April 2025, a study in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences examined mice engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease. In that model, an early rise in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Genetically removing the enzyme that produces D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive problems. This was a different biological setting from the Menin experiments, but it demonstrated that D-serine can have different effects depending on the underlying disease process.

Sources indicate that research published on September 16, 2026, in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease pointed in another direction. In a different Alzheimer's mouse model, a diet enriched with L-serine increased blood levels of both L-serine and D-serine and partially restored measures of new neuron production in the hippocampus. It did not improve the buildup of amyloid, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease. Importantly, this experiment tested L-serine and the production of new neurons, not D-serine supplementation as a treatment for human aging.

Sources indicate that taken together, these findings suggest that serine metabolism is a promising research target, but not a simple case of more being better. The form of serine, the condition being studied, and the outcome being measured all matter. Neither study directly confirms or overturns the original Menin results.

What the Findings Mean for People.

Recent findings suggest that there is some human research on D-serine, although it does not establish an aging treatment. A small randomized study published in 2016, before the Menin work, tested a single dose in 50 healthy older adults. Participants improved on one measure of a computerized maze task, but the researchers found no significant benefit on the other cognitive tests or mood measures. The experiment did not establish lasting memory benefits, slower aging, or the safety of prolonged use in older adults.

According to recent reports, the Menin findings leave several important questions unresolved. Researchers still need to determine what causes the protein to decline with age, how much of the resulting physical and cognitive deterioration can be prevented, and how long any benefits might last. They also need to understand whether altering Menin or supplementing D-serine could produce unintended effects.

The central possibility remains compelling: some changes associated with aging may be influenced by signals originating in a small part of the brain. Understanding those signals could reveal ways to protect function later in life. For now, however, the evidence points to an experimental pathway worth investigating, not a supplement proven to turn back human aging.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar.
  • It has been revealed that “I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” indicates René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing.
  • Recent findings suggest that meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and newly introduced spaces, including three new galleries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar. While the city no longer commands the same international panache it enjoyed before the pandemic, galleries report encouraging early sales, suggesting that committed collectors remain active despite a more cautious market.

It has been revealed that “I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” indicates René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing. He adds that younger collectors increasingly favour artists of their own generation. While established artists continued to attract buyers, collectors were taking longer to commit to expensive works. Meile attributed the shift partly to the departure of speculative buyers from the market.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and newly introduced spaces, including three new galleries. Hangzhou’s longtime fair regular Inna Art Space just opened Inna Front Room in the Lujiazui business district, making it the first significant gallery on the Pudong side of the river. Chen Yongwei, the former director of nonprofit Pond Society, has opened Shanghai Industry atop the Suhe House art cluster. PTT Space, a rising star gallery from Taipei, meanwhile this week opened an outpost at the M50 gallery complex.

Sources indicate that “Even though the Chinese market is at an all-time low, Shanghai is still a vibrant international city with many art institutions,” says Robert Hsu, who founded PTT in 2020. “Considering the past art week, the number of openings parties and fairs is still through the roof, surpassing Seoul Art Week and coming close to Hong Kong Art Week.”.

Hsu states he also has existing “base infrastructure” in the city with staff and relationships with local artists and collectors. “As a second generation gallerist, I feel we have to keep moving in this latest era. The market, the business, the people have all changed. To survive, I have to step out of our comfort zone and explore.”.

Jae Pil Eun's Night Walking, showing at Hang Over.

Courtesy of the artists and SYSTEMA © SYSTEMA, 2026.

Along with the gallery, Hsu is part of the team organising the new boutique fair Art Fusion Canton in the southern Chinese city Guangzhou next month (3-7 December). In Shanghai, the popup fair Hang Over (11-15 November) is going strong in its second year. Moving from last year’s restaurant to an event space in a new lifestyle complex on Donghu Lu, it this year features 18 galleries including Tokyo’s Misako & Rosen, Seoul’s Cylinder along with Shanghai’s Antenna Space, Vanguard and Linseed, owned by Hang Over founder Zhuang Lingzhi.

The 13th edition of West Bund Art & Design (10–15 November) brought together 85 galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Perrotin, Thaddaeus Ropac and White Cube. Meanwhile, the 14th Art021, hosting 111 galleries at the Shanghai Exhibition Centre, has introduced a fresh acquisition initiative with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (Lacma), supported by Chinese collectors, aimed at bringing works by Asian and Asian diaspora artists into the museum’s collection.

At West Bund, Thaddaeus Ropac reports several opening-day sales, led by Megan Rooney’s That Sky (Atlas) (2026), sold for £400,000 to a Chinese foundation. Other transactions included a painting by Martha Jungwirth for €200,000, a Robert Longo work for $90,000 and a painting by Han Bing for €55,000, acquired by an Asian museum. A work by Joan Snyder was also sold to a Chinese museum.

Visitor at West Bund Art & Design 2026.

Courtesy of West Bund Art & Design.

It has been revealed that dawn Zhu, the gallery’s Asia director, praises the enthusiasm of collectors, noting that the gallery had made early sales to both institutions and private collections. “We are seeing collectors who have travelled from across South East Asia and even a few from Europe,” she indicates.

Industry observers note that hauser & Wirth also reports significant sales at West Bund, led by Louise Bourgeois’s bronze sculpture Point of Contact (1967–68, cast 2006), which sold for $450,000 to a museum in Kuala Lumpur. Other transactions include Lee Bul’s Perdu XXXIII (2020), sold for $260,000 to a private collection in China, and another Bourgeois work, Femme (2008), acquired by a Chinese private collector for $165,000. The gallery also reports the sale of George Condo’s Black and Red Composition (2026) for $200,000.

At Art021, Galerie Urs Meile reports sales of works by Xie Nanxing for approximately RMB 1.2m and Ju Ting for RMB 400,000, alongside works by younger artists Chen Zuo and Miao Miao priced between RMB 100,000 and RMB 150,000, and a smaller painting by Vietnamese artist Mai Ta for RMB 40,000.

Also at Art021, Shanghai-based gallery Bank reports strong early sales of Liang Hao’s works, priced 60,000 to 300,000 RMB, and of a large Jiang Cheng painting for over 500,000 RMB. The gallery reports that Lacma may acquire a video work made in 2000 by Los Angeles-based artist Patty Chang.

Despite the more subdued atmosphere, some galleries remain optimistic about the depth of China’s domestic market. Liang Xiao, a spokesperson for Perrotin, which has operated a Shanghai space since 2018, notes that the slowdown had given collectors more time to select works they genuinely appreciate.

He suggests that the growth of latest art fairs in Yokohama, Seoul and elsewhere would not fundamentally undermine Shanghai’s position, given the size of China’s domestic collector base. “Even after all these years, there are still many collectors we have yet to reach,” Liang says, adding that Shanghai remains an important entry point for collectors from across mainland China.

Hsu claims the feedback for PTT Shanghai has been “quite positive” in the debut week, but “the market is not at its best.” Transactions have been slow, but included some successful placement of works with established collectors. “As the old saying goes, the gallery business is a marathon, not a sprint.”.

#91874. How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1519 w)

How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting.
  • While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.
  • Industry observers note that according to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting. During these years, it’s easy to prioritize your child’s grades, sports, and other accolades, especially as they inch toward leaving the nest.

While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.

Industry observers note that according to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers. Research reveals emotional maturity is the ability to accept and express care, temper major feelings, and make wise choices. Without it, teens are more likely to feel lonely and less satisfied with life, one study found.

In her latest book, How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child, Gibson points out that “the quality of humanity’s future depends on the emotional maturity of coming generations.”.

Industry observers note that juli Fraga: In your book, you mention that humanity’s future will depend on emotional maturity. Why does this matter so much right now?

Lindsay Gibson: Emotional maturity is critical to our well-being as individuals and to the smooth, productive, and innovative aspects of society. When you’re emotionally mature, you can think and anticipate consequences. You can also look back and learn from what you’ve done before. So, you can rely on your thinking to help you deal with reality. Emotional maturity also means tuning into your inner world, including your emotions, imagination, hopes, dreams, connections to other people, and sense of belonging.

In a recent development, JF: Our society places a lot of emphasis on achievement, and less importance on emotional intelligence. How can parents help their teens balance the two?

Recent findings suggest that LG: There’s a real cultural pull in society to prize intelligence and achievement. But when parents get too fixated on these qualities, a child may feel like performance matters more than their thoughts, feelings, and sense of safety.

Kids need to be safely held and supported through the growing-up process. It helps them feel resilient, secure, and confident—qualities they need to take out into the world to function independently. If you get too fixated on the intelligence and achievement parts, you’ve got someone who’s very powerful in one area, but whose emotional side may be underdeveloped. It’s the balance between the two that matters.

Sources indicate that JF: In your book, you mention why it’s so important for parents to help their kids develop a sense of self. Can you explain why this matters, especially during the teen years when kids are individuating?

According to recent reports, LG: One way teens find out who they are is by discovering who they’re not. Teens might push a limit or break a rule, and it’s all par for the course. What’s notable for parents is to be able to recognize and imagine that their child has a separate heart and mind from theirs—a process called “mentalization.”.

A self is that inner spark that speaks to us. It indicates “don’t do that” or “now’s the time to go for it.” It guides you toward what’s most compatible with your individuality and who you are meant to be.

Our sense of self comes from our relationships with people we love and who love us. To feel secure, kids need solid, dependable, connected, and deeply resonant relationships with their parents and caretakers. They need parents who are curious and reflect something back that’s meaningful about who the young person is. When they have that foundation, they have a sense of being a real person inside.

Industry observers note that JF: Parents are so busy these days, and overloaded—mentally and emotionally. Raising emotionally mature kids may feel like another substantial to-do on an already long list. What advice do you have?

LG: Taking time to pause and take your child seriously as a real person will work wonders for their self-confidence and future resilience.

Slowing down takes practice because by the time you’re old enough to have a family, you’ve probably been very goal-directed; parents can be pretty hard on themselves because our culture is so fixated on achievement.

But pulling yourself away from your goal for even a second to tend to your child is something worth practicing because that’s what children’s needs are all about. Kids also develop confidence when they know they matter just as much as anybody else.

JF: What are some behaviors that are normal for teens but that parents might misinterpret as pushback or misbehavior?

LG: Sometimes teens experiment with saying or doing things that clash with their socialization up to that point, such as the language they use or the clothes they wear. These are things that the parent can feel like, “Whoa, I’m uncomfortable with this…”.

Here are two meaningful ways to navigate these moments.

Ask your teen questions about what they’re into, such as the styles they like or what they admire about someone they idolize. Try showing interest, not intrusive interest, but just interest in what they like, or why they are experimenting with different things.

Keep in mind that when your teen snaps at you, is in a bad mood, or slams the door, their emotional centers are activated in a way that will probably never be repeated in their life because their brains prioritize emotional development first during this stage.

JF: Can you share more about why a teen’s development follows this trajectory?

LG: Yeah, I know it’s easy to ask, “Why in the world would nature do it that way?” It’s because that’s how vital the emotional self and relationships are to our real success as independent adults.

It has been revealed that as adults, we have to know ourselves inside and out and use our feelings to guide us. Teens are still trying to work this out. Learning how to handle these emotions takes a lot of practice. They’re finding out what it’s like to feel rage, or what it’s like to be in love, or to feel disappointed. And they’re feeling them in the most intense way they ever will, because the brain is taking on the job of developing them into a really deep, complete human being.

JF: What advice do you have for parents when their teen’s emotions push their own buttons?

LG: Keep in mind that when your teen responds in an adamant, emotional, defiant way, or calls you names, they’re not really in command of those emotions yet.

Instead of coming down hard with words that suggest they’re not a good person, try to respond with: “I’m really interested in how you feel about this. I want to hear your arguments, but when you call me a name, it makes it impossible for me to be available to you. It just doesn’t work. We don’t call each other names in this family. That won’t work when you’re an adult, either.”.

According to recent reports, the interaction then becomes an education about how people respond to different kinds of approaches. Harshness that stops a teen cold shuts down their impulse to communicate their feelings to other people, which isn’t good for resilience or honest relationships.

JF: What are two things that parents do to foster emotional maturity that can actually backfire?

LG: One is the importance of achievement, of having a good resume. Of course, parents know how hard life is as an adult. We feel it’s our duty to convey these realizations to our kids. But when it becomes something that feels like everything else will fall into place if you do these things first or achieve X, we are not helping our kids with the emotional or interpersonal side of life. We’re creating a one-dimensional kind of person.

Sometimes parents also think that if they don’t give their child severe consequences or punishments, the child won’t learn and mature. When you try to convey information through punishment, you actually teach a child to defer to other people’s anger and control. Of course, we want them to be aware of consequences, but sometimes we can go too far. You can’t have a full, right life if you’re always anticipating that somebody might be mad at you.

Juli Fraga, Psy.D., is an AEDP-trained psychologist in San Francisco. She supports parents with kids of all ages. She is also the co-author of the new book, Parents Have Feelings, Too.

#91873. Tech Report: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once

📅 21 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (901 w)

Tech Report: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.
  • Researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels.
  • The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.

Researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels. Known as the microfluidic Axialtrode (mAxialtrode), the device is designed to provide multiple functional points along the length of the implant. This allows researchers to record neural activity and deliver medication to specific locations across different parts of the brain.

The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.

A Multifunction Tool for Brain Research.

In a recent development, for now, the technology is primarily intended as a research tool. Scientists could use it to investigate how signals travel through different layers of the brain during processes involving epilepsy, memory, and decision-making.

Over the longer term, the researchers say the mAxialtrode could also have therapeutic applications. One possibility would be using the device to deliver drugs to precise locations while simultaneously applying electrical stimulation or light stimulation to selected areas of the brain.

Postdoc Kunyang Sui, who developed the mAxialtrode concept together with Associate Professor Christos Markos, claims one of the main advantages is that several capabilities can be combined within a single implant. That could allow researchers to perform more precise experiments while reducing the need for multiple devices inserted into the brain.

According to recent reports, "Most current brain implants are based on hard materials such as silicon, which can irritate the brain and trigger inflammatory reactions in the tissue. The fresh implant differs in that it is made of soft, plastic-like optical fibers and has a specially angled tip that makes it smaller and reduces the damage caused when it is placed in the brain," claims Kunyang Sui.

Recent findings suggest that sui cautions that the technology is still far from routine clinical use. Extensive testing, additional development, and regulatory approvals would be required before it could be used to treat patients.

Moving Beyond Conventional Optical Fibers.

Brain researchers at the moment use flat-ended optical fibers in many experiments. These thin fibers, made from glass or plastic, can carry light into deep regions of the brain. They are frequently used in optogenetics, a technique in which specific nerve cells are activated using light.

Conventional fibers, however, have an vital limitation. They typically interact with brain tissue only at the end of the fiber, meaning researchers can stimulate or monitor just one location at a time.

Industry observers note that the outermost end is called the distal tip, or the "nose" of the fiber. Light is emitted and contact with brain tissue occurs only at this point. As a result, scientists may be limited to measuring or stimulating one brain layer at a time, even though many brain functions depend on communication among several layers and deeper structures.

How the New Brain Implant Works.

The needle-thin mAxialtrode begins as a much larger polymer rod. Researchers heat the material and draw it into an extremely thin fiber, somewhat like producing a very fine strand of sugar, but with far greater precision.

A light-conducting core runs through the center of the fiber. Surrounding it are eight microscopic channels that can transport liquids. Those channels can also hold extremely thin metal wires used to measure electrical activity in the brain.

The finished fiber measures less than half a millimeter across. It is also highly flexible, allowing it to move along with brain tissue rather than pressing rigidly through it. This difference in stiffness could be crucial because harder implants can trigger inflammatory responses when they remain in the brain for long periods.

The researchers tested the system not only in the laboratory but also "in vivo," meaning in living mice. The electrode was implanted in the animals' brains and connected to light sources, recording equipment, and small pumps used to deliver fluids.

The experiments showed that the device could stimulate nerve cells using both blue and red light. At the same time, researchers were able to record electrical activity from shallow and deeper brain regions, including the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.

Recent findings suggest that they were also able to inject different substances at separate depths, with delivery points spaced almost three millimeters apart. All of these measurements and forms of stimulation were carried out using a single lightweight fiber, which the mice were able to carry without any obvious signs of discomfort.

Potential Applications in Epilepsy and Neuroscience.

It has been revealed that the in vivo experiments and neurophysiological validation were performed in close collaboration with Associate Professor Rune W. Berg of the University of Copenhagen and Associate Professor Rob C. Wykes from University College London. Their contributions included expertise in analyzing neural circuits and models relevant to epilepsy.

Recent findings suggest that the research team is now working to patent the technology behind the brain electrode. The scientists are also exploring what would be required to begin testing the device in patients within a clinical setting.

Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.

The card is the poster here. The Purple, one of the new card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip. The same violet bleeds into a painted field behind the card, so object and world share one color. Wolff Olins spent time in Seoul before drawing anything, talking with customers and young Koreans. More than eight in ten South Koreans in their twenties still live with their parents, so people define themselves through taste and through what they choose to carry. A card indicates something about who you are and who you intend to become, and that became the design problem.

The system runs on a simple split. A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card. Around that core, each card gets its own world. The entry cards, M, X and Z, use a generative system of bright color and repetition, so no two faces repeat the same pattern. A type specimen sheet sets the grotesque in full, and the card specification drawing marks the 1.58 ratio every face must hold.

According to recent reports, scale does the talking in the applications. The wordmark stays small and bracketed while a single figure, 93 percent, fills a whole green panel, and the card faces run at poster size on street walls. The card ratio repeats across posters, totes and packaging, so the system reads as one object cut to different sizes.

It has been revealed that the physical pieces carry the same discipline. Modular packaging holds the whole range together: a grey box with a debossed Hyundai Card mark and a red peel tab, each card sealed in a protective layer that peels back to reveal its character. The dotted halftone on the Purple card reads as texture before it reads as pattern. The tote bag carries the bracketed wordmark on green, with a black band at the base.

Color is the flex in the system. Violet owns the Purple card, acid green owns the commercial card and the significant figures, and black and grey hold everything together. The butterfly image shows what the generative color does when it leaves the card: the same violet, painted loose across a wing, with the pattern breaking into dots. Every card keeps the same bones and gets a different skin.

Breaking: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep.
  • To investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity.
  • "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep. Some people can have caffeine late in the day and fall asleep easily, while others may remain awake for hours. But researchers are increasingly finding that simply asking whether coffee delays sleep may miss a more important concern: what caffeine does to the brain after sleep begins.

To investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity. EEG measurements can reveal much more than how long someone sleeps or how often they wake up. They can also provide clues about the biological quality and depth of that sleep.

"EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping. Classical sleep assessment assesses sleep duration and its stages, whereas quantitative EEG analysis reveals more subtle changes, such as reduced slow-wave activity, which is an notable marker of sleep depth and its restorative character," explains Prof. Donata Kurpas from the Department of Nursing, Wroclaw Medical University.

Slow waves are a major feature of deep sleep -- the stage associated with physical recovery, replenishing energy reserves, and maintaining healthy brain function.

Caffeine May Make Sleep Less Restorative.

Industry observers note that caffeine does not always affect sleep in obvious ways. A person may still fall asleep at a normal time and remain asleep for what appears to be a full night, yet the quality of that rest may still be altered.

"Caffeine may shorten sleep or make it more difficult to fall asleep; however, even when sleep duration appears normal, it may reduce slow-wave activity and shift the EEG pattern toward a more 'wakeful' brain," states Prof. Kurpas.

In a recent development, in practical terms, someone might spend eight hours in bed without getting the same level of neurological recovery they would normally expect. Because the disruption may not cause obvious awakenings, it can easily go unnoticed.

According to recent reports, "The subjective feeling of having slept well does not always correspond to what we observe in neurophysiological recordings. A person may fall asleep without major difficulty and not remember awakenings, while the brain may display fewer features of deep sleep," the expert adds.

Why Caffeine Affects People Differently.

It has been revealed that another major finding from caffeine research is that responses vary considerably from person to person. Genetics, metabolism, age, stress, and chronic fatigue can all influence how strongly caffeine affects sleep.

For some people, even coffee consumed early in the day may still have an impact by nighttime.

Industry observers note that "It is not only about coffee consumed just before bedtime. For some people, the total amount of caffeine consumed during the day and whether the body has enough time to metabolize it before nightfall may also be vital," Prof. Kurpas emphasizes.

That possibility may be especially relevant for people who rely on caffeine to improve focus, stamina, or performance, including athletes, people doing mentally demanding work, and anyone who regularly uses coffee or other caffeinated products to stay alert.

Caffeine Can Create a Fatigue Cycle.

According to recent reports, caffeine can temporarily increase alertness and make fatigue feel less noticeable. However, experts caution that the boost may sometimes come at the expense of the body's ability to recover fully during sleep.

It has been revealed that in that sense, caffeine can resemble "borrowing energy" from the body. If nighttime recovery becomes less effective, the person may feel more tired the following day and turn to even more caffeine for help.

"If caffeine helps a person function during the day while simultaneously worsening the quality of nighttime recovery, a vicious circle may develop: greater fatigue, greater need for stimulation, and poorer sleep," notes Prof. Kurpas.

In a recent development, these findings are one reason sleep researchers are paying less attention to sleep duration alone. Increasingly, the focus is shifting toward what the brain is actually doing during the night and whether that sleep is biologically restorative.

It has been revealed that "Caffeine is neither 'good' nor 'bad'. It is a biologically active substance whose effects depend on dose, time of day, age, lifestyle, sleep quality, stress burden, and individual sensitivity," the expert concludes.
